episodes.episode: UK Railway Mania: parliamentary authorization boom, 1845-46 flotation frenzy, 1847 commercial crisis, 1848-50 dividend collapse
episodes.period: 1843-1850 (incumbent scarcity-rent era 1830-1845; share peak Oct 1845; capex peak 1847; trough Apr 1850)
episodes.bottleneck: Point-to-point land transport capacity between industrial cities. Railways had a ~10x speed and large cost advantage over canals/turnpikes, and each route was a de facto natural monopoly until Parliament authorized a competing line. Rents were pure route-toll rents: Liverpool & Manchester (opened 1830) averaged 9.5% annual dividends over 15 years of independent existence; London & Birmingham, Grand Junction, York & North Midland also paid ~10% — the ceiling permitted by their acts. These 10% yields, vs ~3% consols, were the scarcity signal that triggered the mania.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Miles authorized vs demand-consistent: ~2,000 route-miles open in 1843; Parliament authorized ~9,500-9,800 miles in 1844-50 (96% in 1844-47: 2,816 miles in 1845; 272 Acts / 4,540 miles in 1846 vs 4,039 miles authorized in ALL of 1821-44; authorizations collapsed to 16 miles in 1849 and 7 in 1850). Of the authorized mileage, 3,762 miles (38%) was formally abandoned per the 1856 Board of Trade report — i.e., authorization overshoot ratio ~1.6x what was ultimately built and roughly 3x the pre-existing network. Capex flow overshoot: peak-year 1847 spend £44M ≈ 7% of GDP and roughly half of all UK domestic fixed investment, vs a sustainable ~£10-15M/yr; total decade spend ~£250M ≈ half a year's national output; 1846 authorized capital commitments alone ~£132M ≈ half national income. Capacity vs demand at trough: network tripled while traffic tripled too, but revenue per mile and ROE halved — effective capacity ~2x the level that would have preserved pre-boom returns.

equity_outcomes.name: All-railway share index (Campbell)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Rose 106.2% Jan 1843 (=1000) to 2,062 on 6 Oct 1845; fell 20.2% in ~5 weeks; long grind down to 741 by Apr 1850; shares fell below pre-boom par

equity_outcomes.name: Mania-cohort new lines (pure capacity, no traffic base)
equity_outcomes.outcome: 38% of authorized mileage abandoned; many companies wound up, absorbed at distressed prices by trunk lines, or exposed as frauds; holders of £10-paid £50 shares faced 90% capital calls, often losing more than initial outlay

equity_outcomes.name: George Hudson companies (York & North Midland, Eastern Counties, Midland etc.)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Hudson controlled ~1/4 of network; 1849 shareholder committees exposed dividends paid from capital and inflated valuations; Hudson ruined, fled abroad; his companies' shares among worst performers

equity_outcomes.name: Established trunk lines (LNWR formed 1846, Great Western)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Dividends compressed from ~10% to ~4-6% but stayed solvent; consolidated the network by absorbing failed mania lines cheaply; sector ROE 5.07% (1844) to 2.37% (1849) and never returned to pre-mania levels

equity_outcomes.name: Contractors (Thomas Brassey; Peto, Brassey & Betts)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Cost-plus builders captured the capex flow, not the capacity risk; Brassey built 1/3 of UK network by 1847, survived, went global (~8,500 miles lifetime, 1 in 20 of world rail miles); Peto survived until the separate 1866 Overend Gurney crisis

key_numbers: Incumbent scarcity rents: L&M averaged 9.5%/yr dividends for 15 yrs (1830-45) vs consols ~3% — a ~6.5pp excess return sustained until the supply wave
Authorizations: 1844 petitions 199, 1845 562, 1846 815; miles authorized 1845: 2,816; 1846: 4,540 (272 Acts); vs 4,039 total in 1821-44; 1849: 16 miles; 1850: 7 miles

Capex: 1843-50 total £109M actually spent within the period, ~£250M over the decade including completion tail; 1847 peak £44M/yr ≈ 7% of GDP, >2x the military budget; ~250,000 navvies employed at peak (~4% of male workforce)
Share index: +106.2% Jan 1843-Oct 1845; -64.1% Oct 1845-Apr 1850; first leg down -20.2% in ~5 weeks

Sector dividends on paid-up capital: 7.2% Jul 1847 -> 6.3% Apr 1848 -> 5.5% Oct 1848 -> 4.4% Apr 1849 -> 3.5% Oct 1849 -> 2.9% Dec 1850 (common-share average ~1.9% in 1849); ROE 5.07% (1844) -> 2.37% (1849)
Demand DID materialize: passengers 24.5M (1842) -> 72.9M (1850), ~3x in 8 years — the bust came from supply growing faster than a genuinely tripling demand, not from demand failure
Abandonment: 3,762 of 9,800 authorized miles (38%) never built (Board of Trade 1856); network open ~6,000 miles by 1850, ~7,300 by 1852 vs ~2,000 in 1843
Credit event: BoE bullion drained by 1846 famine grain imports + railway calls; 'Week of Terror' 17-23 Oct 1847, four banks failed; Bank Charter Act suspended 25 Oct 1847

Financing: 100% equity (no bond market for new lines), but partly-paid shares (10% deposit on e.g. £50 nominal) = 10:1 embedded leverage; post-1846 calls on the remaining 90% ran ~£40M/yr and forced distressed selling for years
episodes.glut_depth: Returns on capital roughly halved and never recovered to pre-boom levels: sector ROE fell from 5.07% (1844) to 2.37% (1849); dividends on paid-up capital from 7.2% (Jul 1847) to ~1.9-2.9% (1849-50), i.e., below the consol yield — railway capital earned negative spread over the risk-free rate at the trough. Share index bottomed 26% below its Jan 1843 pre-boom level. The glut was permanent in returns terms (UK railways never again paid 10%) but the physical capacity was fully absorbed: traffic kept compounding and the 1850s network became the backbone of the economy. Duplicate/competing routes kept per-mile pricing power suppressed for decades.
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Peak signal: established lines paying the statutory-maximum 10% dividends (L&M avg 9.5% over 15 yrs) against 3-3.4% consols — a 3x yield multiple — plus BoE discount rate at a then-record-low 2.5% in 1844 (Bank Charter Act year), pushing yield-starved savers into railway scrip. Scrip premiums: partly-paid shares of unbuilt lines traded at large premiums to deposits in 1845 (effective 2-10x gains on 10% deposits within months). Sector dividend peak: 7.2% on paid-up capital, July 1847 — note dividends peaked ~21 months AFTER share prices peaked (Oct 1845).
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Demand largely materialized — this is the canonical 'right about the technology, wrong about the returns' episode. Passenger journeys 24.5M (1842) -> 72.9M (1850), ~13%/yr compound; freight similarly transformed; rail became indispensable. But promoters' prospectuses promised ~10% dividends on every line (extrapolating L&M monopoly economics to competitive branch lines); realized sector returns were 2-3%. Roughly: demand delivered ~3x growth, capacity delivered ~3x growth plus duplication and higher-cost routes, so unit economics collapsed even as volume forecasts were met or beaten. Promised returns overshot realized by ~3-4x.
episodes.financing_structure: Essentially all external equity from a newly broadened retail/middle-class investor base (clergy, widows, tradesmen — plus MPs: ~157 members of Parliament held railway interests), via partly-paid shares: 10% deposit on nominal capital (deposit required by Parliament to be lodged before an Act), remaining 90% subject to calls at the directors' discretion. This is equity in name but functions as 10:1 leverage with recourse — the model should treat it as debt-like. Almost no bonds for new lines; established companies later issued some debentures. Banks amplified by lending against scrip. Credit tightening's role: real but secondary as trigger, primary as amplifier. The share-price peak (Oct 1845) preceded monetary stress; proximate pinpricks were the Nov 1845 Board of Trade registration deadline revealing 1,200+ planned schemes, and rising call schedules. Then 1846-47 Irish famine grain imports drained BoE gold, discount rate rose from 2.5% (1844) through 1846-47 to crisis levels, and calls (~£40M/yr) collided with tight money: April 1847 squeeze, then the October 1847 'Week of Terror' (four bank failures, Bank Charter Act suspended by government letter of 25 Oct 1847). Companies kept calling capital into the downturn to finish half-built lines — capex momentum continued ~2 years past the equity peak. Hudson's 1849 fraud exposure (dividends paid out of capital) ended residual credibility.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS: (1) Contractors selling capex itself — Brassey, Peto (cost-plus, took payment partly in shares/bonds post-bust, i.e., became financiers when capital dried up); Brassey died rich in 1870. (2) Consolidated trunk operators with network/route moats — LNWR (1846 amalgamation), Midland, GWR: absorbed distressed mania lines at cents on the pound, kept 4-6% dividends; the moat was the route franchise + amalgamation scale, not the steel. (3) Suppliers of scarce inputs during the build (iron, land — landowners extracted premium prices via compulsory-purchase negotiations). COMPETED AWAY / CASUALTIES: pure-capacity new entrants duplicating routes (38% of authorized miles abandoned, near-total equity losses); leveraged retail holders of partly-paid scrip (calls exceeded ability to pay); promoters and the 'Railway King' George Hudson (fraud exposed 1849, ruined); banks exposed to scrip lending (Oct 1847 failures). Mapping to AI capex: contractors ≈ Nvidia/TSMC/EPC firms; trunk amalgamators ≈ hyperscalers with distribution moats absorbing distressed datacenter capacity; mania cohort ≈ neocloud/pure-GPU-capacity entrants.

lessons_for_model: Rent-duration calibration, two regimes: (a) incumbent/monopoly regime before entry is possible: ~15 years of ~3x risk-free returns (9.5% vs 3% consols, 1830-1845) — supply response delayed by authorization friction (Parliament) and 3-4 yr construction time; (b) once entry floodgates open, rents die in ~4-6 years: scarcity signal fully visible 1843-44, dividend peak Jul 1847, normalization to sub-risk-free by 1849. Model: rent half-life ~2 yrs after competing capacity starts landing.

Supply-response delay: authorization-to-revenue lag 3-4 years (1845-46 Acts -> lines opening 1848-50). Capex-momentum loop: spending peaked 1847, TWO YEARS after the equity-price peak (Oct 1845), because sunk half-built projects forced continued calls. Calibrate capex momentum so peak capex lags peak valuation by ~2 yrs and continues ~1-2 yrs into falling marginal returns.

Overshoot ratio targets: authorized/announced capacity ~1.6x actually-built (38% abandonment rate — model should let ~1/3-40% of announced projects cancel); built capacity ~2x demand-consistent-at-old-margins; peak-year capex ~3-4x sustainable run-rate (£44M vs ~£12M) and ~7% of GDP.

Demand loop: demand is NOT the failure mode — volume tripled (24.5M->72.9M passengers, ~13%/yr CAGR) yet returns halved permanently. The model must be able to produce a bust with realized demand at or above forecast, purely from supply outrunning it and duplication destroying pricing power. Promised returns / realized returns ≈ 3-4x (10% promised, 2-3% realized).

Return trajectory to reproduce: sector ROE 5.07% (1844) -> 2.37% (1849); dividends on paid-up capital 7.2% (Jul 1847) -> 2.9% (Dec 1850), crossing BELOW the risk-free rate at trough. Post-glut returns never recovered to pre-boom levels — permanent competitive regime shift, not a cycle around a fixed mean.

Equity path: +106% in ~2.75 yrs, then -64% over 4.5 yrs (first leg -20% in 5 weeks, then slow grind — NOT a single crash). Index trough 26% below pre-boom start. Bust lag: peak capex (1847) to systemic credit event (Oct 1847) < 1 yr; to full margin normalization ~2-3 yrs; to price trough (Apr 1850) ~3 yrs.

Credit-discipline loop: financing was nominally 100% equity but partly-paid shares = 10:1 embedded recourse leverage; capital CALLS (~£40M/yr 1846-49) acted as forced procyclical deleveraging of households. Credit tightening (BoE gold drain from famine imports + rate hikes 1846-47, Bank Charter Act suspended 25 Oct 1847) AMPLIFIED and dated the bust but did not initiate it — the equity peak preceded monetary stress by a year. Model: credit crunch as accelerant with ~2-yr lag after valuation peak, and margin-call/committed-capex mechanics as the key household->macro transmission.

Rent allocation for survivors: capex-flow sellers (contractors ≈ Nvidia/TSMC analog) kept ~100% of their rents through the bust — their revenue tracks the capex flow, so model their peak-to-trough revenue as proportional to the capex decline (~60-70% fall after 1847) but with no balance-sheet destruction; franchise/network incumbents kept ~50% of prior rents via consolidation (bought distressed capacity at deep discounts); pure-capacity entrants lost 100%, worse than -100% for called partly-paid holders.

Sentiment/authorization proxy for the model's expectation loop: petitions 199 (1844) -> 562 (1845) -> 815 (1846) -> authorizations 16 miles (1849): a ~3x/yr growth in project announcements for 2 years, then >99% collapse within 3 years — use announced-project flow as the overshoot state variable with ~2-yr boom persistence.

Fraud/accounting channel: peak-era dividends were partly paid out of capital (Hudson), overstating margins at exactly the moment supply was landing — model should allow reported margins to exceed true margins by 2-3pp near the peak, with discovery (1849) as a second-leg-down trigger.

episodes.episode: US railroads 1865-1895: transcontinental land-grant boom, 1873 and 1893 panics, receivership wave, Morganization
episodes.bottleneck: Trunk-line and transcontinental route capacity — the physical right-of-way plus completed track between traffic-generating termini. Pre-1873 east-west trunk capacity and the single Pacific route (UP/CP, completed May 1869) earned monopoly tolls on all overland freight/passengers. Rents were amplified by federal subsidy: 131.2M acres of federal land grants (patented) plus ~49M state acres, and US bonds of $16,000/$32,000/$48,000 per mile by terrain under the Pacific Railway Acts.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Mileage grew 35,000 (1865) → 52,900 (1870) → ~70,000 (1873) → 93,200 (1880) → 163,600 (1890) → ~176,000 (1893). Cycle 1: 29,589 miles added 1868-73 (annual build records every year 1869-72, peak 7,439 miles in 1872 = ~12%/yr capacity growth) against demand growing far slower; ~half of roads defaulted by 1876. Cycle 2: 70,400 miles added 1880-90, peak 12,876 miles in 1887; by 1893-97 firms owning 25-33% of ALL US mileage went through receivership — i.e., roughly one-third of installed capacity was demand-inconsistent at prevailing rates. Effective overshoot ratio ~1.4-1.5x demand-consistent capacity (proxied by bankrupt-mileage share plus parallel-line redundancy: West Shore duplicated NY Central and was bankrupt within ~2 years of completion, 1883-85; Nickel Plate duplicated Lake Shore). Peak-year build rate was ~2.5-3x the sustainable absorption rate (~4,000-5,000 miles/yr of the 1890s-1900s).

key_numbers: Annual build: 7,439 mi peak 1872 → ~1,600 mi trough 1875 (-78% in 3 yrs); 12,876 mi peak 1887 → ~1,900 mi trough 1895 (-85% in 8 yrs)
1868-1873: 29,589 miles added; every year 1869-72 a new construction record
Federal land grants patented: 131,230,358 acres; Pacific Railway Act bonds $16k/$32k/$48k per mile by terrain

Panic of 1873: Jay Cooke & Co failed Sept 18, 1873; 89 of 364 railroads bankrupt within a year; ~half of all roads in default/receivership by 1876; NBER contraction 65 months (Oct 1873 - Mar 1879), longest on record

Panic of 1893: 74 roads in receivership by end-1893; 150+ companies with 30,000+ miles and ~$2.5B capitalization bankrupt in first year; ~200 railroads / 41,000 miles total in receivership; 25-33% of ALL US mileage through bankruptcy 1893-97

Freight rates: Central Pacific 5.95 cents/ton-mile (1870) → 1.83 (1885); Union Pacific 4.26 → 1.49; US average revenue/ton-mile ~2.2 cents (1870) → ~0.94 (1890) → ~0.73 (1900): a 60-70% real price collapse
Returns: railroad bond yields ~6% and dividend yields ~7% circa 1870 → 3.3% and 3.5% by 1900; only 30-40% of railroad stock paid ANY dividend in the 1890s
Railroads absorbed 15-20% of total US national investment in the 1870s-1880s

Credit Mobilier construction-company skim on Union Pacific: ~$23-50M excess profits; dividends to insiders reportedly >300% cumulative — capex itself was the profit center, decoupling build decisions from traffic economics

Morganization 1893-1898: Southern Railway, Erie, Reading, Northern Pacific reorganized — foreclose, cut fixed charges ~30-40% via debt-to-equity conversion, assess shareholders, install voting trust; by 1906 ~two-thirds of US mileage controlled by seven groups
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Circa 1865-1873: dividend yields ~7% vs bond yields ~6%, with strong roads paying 8-10% dividends; land-grant transcontinental private returns of ~11-12% (Central Pacific system, Mercer's estimates) vs ~6% cost of debt; Credit Mobilier insider returns of 3x+ on construction capital. Transcontinental corridor was a pure monopoly toll 1869-1883 (until Northern Pacific and Santa Fe reached the Pacific). Rate signal: trunk-line rates before the 1874-77 rate wars were roughly 3x the 1890 level.
episodes.glut_depth: Rates fell 60-70% (2.2 cents/ton-mile 1870 → 0.94 by 1890, 0.73 by 1900) and never recovered; one-third of national mileage in bankruptcy 1893-97; western land-grant roads ran through unsettled territory at a fraction of designed utilization for 10-20 years ('build ahead of demand'); parallel eastern lines (West Shore, Nickel Plate) drove pricing to marginal cost because fixed charges were ~2/3 of total cost, making price wars rational for any road with idle capacity. Cartels (SRSA 1875, trunk-line pools) repeatedly formed and collapsed — private supply discipline failed until the bankruptcy wave physically transferred control.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Demand was REAL but LATE. Promised: land grants premised on rapid settlement generating traffic ('the railroad creates its own demand'). Realized: ton-miles compounded ~7-9%/yr for decades and the system eventually ran near capacity in the 1900s-1910s — but capacity built in 1869-1873 and 1880-1887 was not traffic-justified until roughly 10-20 years after construction. Northern Pacific's 1870-73 build through empty territory had essentially zero near-term traffic (hence 1875 bankruptcy); the same corridor was profitable by the mid-1890s under Hill/Morgan. The technology delivered its promised deflation (rates -70%) — but that consumer surplus came out of investor returns.
episodes.financing_structure: Overwhelmingly EXTERNAL and DEBT-led for new construction: mortgage bonds typically 50-60%+ of capitalization, sold ahead of any revenue; par capitalization watered to roughly 2x real invested cost. Government de-risked the equity: 131M federal acres + $16-48k/mile in US bonds. Foreign (mainly British, also Dutch/German) capital held roughly $3B of US railroad securities by the early 1890s — on the order of one-third of railroad capital. Construction-company structures (Credit Mobilier for UP, Contract & Finance Co for CP) let insiders extract profit from the CAPEX FLOW rather than from operations, a key overshoot amplifier. Established dense-traffic roads (PRR, NYC) financed largely from retained earnings and survived. CREDIT TIGHTENING ENDED BOTH BOOMS: 1873 — Vienna crash May 1873 shut the European bond window, Cooke could not place NP paper, boom died within 4 months; 1890-93 — Baring crisis (Nov 1890) cut British capital exports, gold outflows and silver-standard fears drained reserves, panic May-July 1893. In both cases the demand shortfall was chronic and visible for years; it was the loss of external FINANCING, not a demand revelation, that stopped construction.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS (moat = franchise corridor + traffic density + low fixed charges, i.e., toll positions): Pennsylvania RR and New York Central (irreplaceable eastern trunk corridors, continuous dividends), Great Northern (lowest-cost route, no land-grant debt, only 1893-solvent transcontinental), Chicago Burlington & Quincy / Chicago & North Western (dense granger networks), and post-1893 the reorganizers themselves — J.P. Morgan & Co and Kuhn Loeb captured the durable rents of the CONSOLIDATION layer (fees, voting trusts, board control), analogous to IP/platform rents. COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity, no moat): speculative transcontinentals (UP, NP, ATSF — all in 1893 receivership), parallel duplicates (West Shore, Nickel Plate — sold to incumbents at distressed prices), thin-traffic granger and southern roads. Rule extracted: rents accrued to route scarcity and terminal control, never to mileage per se; once a second and third road served a corridor, price went to marginal cost. Rents were only restored by ownership consolidation (by 1906 seven groups controlled ~2/3 of mileage) plus regulatory rate stabilization (ICC 1887, strengthened 1903-06).
lessons_for_model: RENT DURATION: 8 years base case (scarcity onset ~1865 postwar traffic boom → trunk-line rate wars 1874-77 normalize margins); use 14 years for a true single-route monopoly (transcontinental toll 1869 → second/third Pacific routes complete 1883). Model rents as killed by ENTRANT COMPLETION events, not gradual erosion: rates step down ~30-50% per completed parallel entrant.
SUPPLY-RESPONSE DELAY: 3-5 years from rent signal to competing capacity in service (charter/finance/build). Calibrate construction pipeline delay ~4 years.

CAPEX MOMENTUM/OVERSHOOT: peak build rate 2.5-3x sustainable absorption; total installed capacity overshoots demand-consistent level by ~1.4-1.5x (validated by 25-33% of mileage passing through bankruptcy 1893-97). Committed projects finish 1-2 years past the credit break (build fell only gradually 1873-74 despite September 1873 panic).

BUST LAG: 1-6 years from peak capex to systemic bust. Cycle 1: peak build 1872 → panic Sept 1873 (~1.5 yr). Cycle 2: peak build 1887 → panic May 1893 (6 yr), with an intermediate credit warning (Baring, Nov 1890) 3 years before the bust. Model should allow a long plateau when credit stays open.

CREDIT-DISCIPLINE LOOP IS THE BINDING CUTOFF: both booms were ended by exogenous credit tightening (Vienna 1873; Baring 1890 + gold drain 1893), not by demand data. External capital ≈1/3 of funding; its withdrawal cut annual capex 78-85% within 3-8 years. Give the credit loop a sharp threshold/nonlinear gain, and make capex nearly insensitive to demand signals while credit is open — construction-company structures (Credit Mobilier) meant builders profited from capex flow itself.

PRICE DYNAMICS IN GLUT: with fixed charges ~2/3 of cost, competition drives price toward marginal cost: rates -60 to -70% over 20 years, permanently. Cartels/pools provide only transient (1-3 yr) price support before defection — do not model voluntary supply discipline as stable.

RENT RESTORATION VIA CONSOLIDATION: post-bust reorganization (Morganization 1893-98) cuts fixed charges 30-40% (debt→equity), transfers assets at ~30-60% of invested cost, and restores oligopoly rents ~5-10 years after the bust (seven groups, 2/3 of mileage by 1906). Model a consolidation phase where surviving/acquiring entities earn normalized returns on WRITTEN-DOWN capital, not original cost.

DEMAND CATCH-UP: underlying demand compounds ~7-9%/yr and fills the overbuilt capacity 10-20 years after peak construction; the bust is a financing/timing failure, not a demand fiction. Calibrate demand-realization lag ~10-15 years behind capacity.

RETURN COMPRESSION TARGET: sector dividend yield 7% → 3.5% and share of dividend-paying equity → 30-40% at trough; equity drawdowns -85 to -100% for pure-capacity players, -25 to -40% for toll/franchise incumbents. Reproduce this bimodal outcome distribution.

WHO KEEPS RENTS: assign durable rents only to agents with route/terminal scarcity (analog: IP, ecosystem lock-in, distribution chokepoints) and to the consolidation/financing layer; assign zero terminal rents to undifferentiated capacity even when the technology's demand promise is ultimately fulfilled.

episodes.episode: US electrification boom: central-station power, utility holding-company pyramid, and electrical equipment duopoly (Insull era through PUHCA)
episodes.period: 1898-1935 (franchise/scarcity era 1898-1907; regulated growth boom 1907-1929; peak capex 1929-30; bust 1931-33; regulatory reset 1935)
episodes.bottleneck: Central-station generating capacity + distribution franchise (natural-monopoly toll). Upstream bottleneck: turbine/generator equipment and patents held by the GE-Westinghouse duopoly (1896 cross-license patent pool). Scale economies (Insull's mass-production-of-kWh model) meant the constraint migrated from 'any capacity at all' (1890s) to 'cheapest large-unit capacity + load diversity' (1910s-20s), then to capital access itself (1920s holding-company era).
episodes.capex_overshoot: Capacity doubled 1920-1930 (+100%) built to a ~7-8%/yr demand-growth extrapolation (generation grew 20x 1902-1930, ~11%/yr). Actual demand: total generation ~116-117 bn kWh 1929 -> ~99 bn kWh 1932 (-15%; utility kWh sales ~-14%; utility output index 100 -> 92.7). Capacity kept RISING through 1932 as the 1929-30 pipeline completed, so peak capacity was ~1.35-1.45x demand-consistent capacity at trough; effective reserve margins hit ~40%+ vs normal ~15%. The overhang took until ~1940 to absorb: 1930s capacity growth only +25% vs +100% in the 1920s, and generation regained the 1929 level in 1935 (index 108.2).
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Long-run demand promise was REAL and over-delivered: generation x20 from 1902-1930; 84% of urban homes electrified by 1930; US generated more power than the rest of the world combined by 1929. But short-run: 1929-32 kWh fell ~15% against plans assuming +7-8%/yr — a 3-year, ~35-40 percentage-point gap vs trend. Demand recovered to the 1929 level in 6 years (1935), yet equity holders of leveraged structures were already wiped out by year 3. Rural demand (12% of farms electrified 1935) was ultimately served by federal REA, not the boom-era private sector.
episodes.glut_depth: Reserve margins ~40%+ vs ~15% normal at 1932-33 trough; utility capacity factor fell from ~32% to ~25-26%; capex (utility construction) down ~70-80% peak-to-trough (economy-wide construction -78% 1929-33); glut absorbed by demand growth over ~7-8 years (1932-1940), aided by near-zero private capacity additions and New Deal hydro taking 20% of 1931-41 additions.
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Real price of electricity fell >80% 1890-1920 and kept falling (avg US price $4.79/kWh in 2019$ in 1902 -> $0.32 by 1950) — rents were passed to consumers via scale economies, not held as margin. The 'margin' signal migrated to the financial layer: holding-company ROE stacking (Insull apex: <$1M controlling $2.5bn, i.e. $2,500 of assets per $1 at apex, per EBSCO/Chicagology); utility stocks priced as growth stocks into 1929 (Dow Utilities peak Sept 1929); regulated operating ROE pinned at ~7-8% from 1907 commissions onward.

equity_outcomes.outcome: -92.67% 1929-1932; uniquely, final low not until 1942 (11.5 yrs after peak) — regulated-toll cash flows survived but equity repriced permanently after PUHCA 1935 broke the pyramids

equity_outcomes.name: General Electric (equipment duopoly, IP moat)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Stock 358 (9/1929) -> 9.5 (6/1932) despite staying profitable EVERY year (sales -67% peak-to-trough, $415M 1929 rev, still $13M profit in 1933, $27M by 1935, dividend raised 1935). Survived intact, kept duopoly rents for decades

equity_outcomes.name: Westinghouse (equipment #2)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Sales -69%; ~$20M cumulative losses over 3 years pre-1935; recovered to ~$12M profit 1935; survived. Drawdown ~-95%

equity_outcomes.name: Insull Middle West Utilities + Insull Utility Investments/Corporation Securities (leveraged capacity aggregator)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Total loss. $3-4bn empire (95+ holding cos, 255 operating cos, 5,000 communities, 32 states) into receivership April 1932 after failing to roll $10M of short-term notes; ~$650M bond default; ~600k-2M retail investors wiped out

equity_outcomes.name: Utility holding companies as a class
equity_outcomes.outcome: 53 holding companies with $1.7bn of securities into bankruptcy/receivership 1929-1936; PUHCA 1935 'death sentence' clause dismantled the survivors

equity_outcomes.name: Regulated operating utilities (the physical toll)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Operationally fine: kWh sales only -14%, revenues down modestly, most kept paying dividends (e.g. Commonwealth Edison never missed one); the assets never stopped earning their regulated ~7% — losses were concentrated in the leverage above them

episodes.financing_structure: Overwhelmingly EXTERNAL and layered: operating utilities ~50-60% mortgage bonds + preferred sold heavily to retail; above them, 2-5 layers of holding companies each adding debt/preferred against the equity below (Insull apex leverage: <$1M directing $2.5bn of assets; two super-holding cos, $250M Utility Investments + $150M Corporation Securities, cross-invested in each other). Utility issues were among the largest categories of 1920s new capital issues. Credit tightening DID end the boom: the 1931-32 bond-market freeze and banks calling stock-collateralized loans meant Middle West could not roll $10M of short-term notes in April 1932 against a $3bn asset base — a 0.3%-of-assets liquidity failure toppling the whole pyramid. Sequence: demand shock (1930-31) -> collateral-value spiral -> refinancing lockout (1931-32) -> default cascade. Equipment makers (GE) were conservatively financed from internal cash and never faced a funding event.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS: (1) GE/Westinghouse — IP/patent-pool duopoly on turbines, generators, lamps; sold shovels to both boom and New Deal; GE profitable every Depression year; duopoly persisted 50+ more years. (2) Regulated operating utilities — legal franchise toll, inelastic demand (-14% vs -50% for industrials), regulated ~7-8% ROE restored by 1935-36. COMPETED/BLOWN AWAY: (1) Holding-company pyramids — pure financial leverage on commodity capacity, zero incremental moat, 100% loss (Insull, 53 bankruptcies, PUHCA dissolution). (2) Isolated small generators — 3,600+ plants in 1902 consolidated away by scale economics; municipal/independent stations absorbed or marginalized. Pattern: the physical asset with a toll survived; the leverage and the aggregation premium above it died; the IP layer above the equipment never even flinched operationally, though its stock still fell 97%.
key_numbers: Generation x20 from 1902-1930 (~11%/yr); 114 bn kWh by 1930; US > rest of world combined by 1929
Real price/kWh: -80%+ 1890-1920; $4.79 (2019$) 1902 -> $0.32 by 1950 — supply response passed nearly all rents to consumers
State regulation converted rents to tolls fast: first commissions (WI, NY) 1907, ~9 yrs after Insull's 1898 NELA speech inviting regulation; regulated ROE ~7-8%
Demand shock: total generation 116-117 bn kWh (1929) -> ~99 bn (1932), -15%; recovered 1929 level by 1935 (output index 100 -> 92.7 -> 108.2)
Capex bust: construction spending -78% 1929-33; New Deal hydro = 20% of all 1931-41 capacity additions
Insull: 95 holding cos + 255 operating cos; <$1M controlling $2.5bn ($2,500 asset per apex $1); $10M unrollable notes killed $3bn Middle West, receivership 8 Apr 1932; $650M bond default
53 holding cos / $1.7bn securities bankrupt 1929-36; PUHCA + Federal Power Act 1935
Equities: Dow Utilities -92.7% (low 1929->1932, FINAL low 1942); GE -97.4% (358->9.5) while profitable every year; GE sales -67%, Westinghouse -69%; Insull equity/juniors -100%
GE 1929: $415M revenue, $70M profit; 1933: $13M profit; 1935: $27M profit, dividend raised
lessons_for_model: Scarcity-rent half-life ~10 yrs when the bottleneck is reproducible capacity: model should kill unregulated capacity rents within 9-15 yrs of onset via entry + regulation (1898->1907 commissions); thereafter cap capacity-owner ROE at a regulated/competitive 7-8% toll

Supply-response loop gain: capacity growth ~2x demand-trend sensitivity at peak — capacity +100%/decade against realized demand that could go -15% in 3 yrs; calibrate overshoot ratio 1.35-1.45x demand-consistent capacity at bust trough
Capex-momentum delay: capacity ADDITIONS kept arriving 2-3 yrs after the demand break (pipeline completion through 1932) — build a 2-3 yr construction/commitment lag that cannot be cancelled
Bust lag: peak capex (1930) -> credit event (Apr 1932) -> capex trough (1933) = 2.5-3 yrs; glut absorption = 7-8 yrs of near-zero net additions (matches telecom 2001-08, useful cross-check)

Credit-discipline loop is the trigger, demand is the fuse: a 0.3%-of-assets refinancing failure ($10M vs $3bn) ended the boom — model default as f(short-term rollover need, collateral value), not f(operating cash flow); operating cash flows fell only ~14%

Leverage stratification: identical physical assets produced -14% revenue at the operating layer and -100% equity 2-3 layers up; the model's equity-outcome module must apply drawdown at the leverage layer, not the asset layer (apex leverage up to 2,500:1)

IP/duopoly layer decouples operationally but not in price: equipment-maker profits stayed positive through a -67% revenue shock, yet stock still fell 97% — model should separate cash-flow survival (moat) from valuation drawdown (beta ~1.1x of bubble index)

Long-run demand over-delivers, short-run kills: allow demand to eventually exceed the boom-era forecast (1935+ recovery, x6 more growth 1945-65) while still bankrupting boom-era leverage — 'right about the future, dead before it arrives'

Rent-repricing is permanent for the toll layer after a political reset: Dow Utilities' real low in 1942 and PUHCA show regulatory backlash adds a second, slower drawdown leg (~5-10 yrs) after the credit bust — include a policy-response feedback with ~3-6 yr lag (crash 1929/32 -> PUHCA 1935)

AI-analog mapping: GPU/chip IP layer = GE/Westinghouse (survives, keeps duopoly rents); datacenter/compute capacity = operating utilities (toll if contracted/regulated, commodity if merchant); leveraged neocloud/SPV aggregators = Insull pyramids (first and total casualty)

episodes.episode: US Radio boom-bust: broadcasting/receiver manufacturing mania, RCA valuation cycle, set-maker shakeout, patent-pool tolls
episodes.period: 1920-1932 (KDKA first broadcast Nov 2, 1920; RCA stock trough May 1932; industry revenue trough 1932-33)
episodes.bottleneck: Two-layer bottleneck. (1) Physical: assembled receiver capacity during the 1922-24 'radio craze' — sets were scarce, waiting lists common, avg set >$200 in 1924; anyone who could assemble a tuned-RF set earned fat margins. This layer had near-zero entry barriers (assembly from purchased parts) and rents died in ~3 years. (2) Legal/IP: the RCA patent pool (GE+Westinghouse+AT&T+United Fruit cross-licenses, ~2,000 patents incl. Armstrong superheterodyne and the triode) — every legitimate set maker needed an RCA package license at 7.5% of set sales price (min ~$100k/yr per licensee); ~25 licensees early 1920s, 155 licensed+unlicensed makers counted in early 1932. The toll layer was the only durable rent.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Firm-count overshoot: 600-1,200 firms assembled/sold receivers in the mid-1920s vs 18 manufacturers/assemblers still in business by 1934 — a 33-65x overshoot in entrants vs sustainable structure (~97-98% attrition). Capacity vs demand: Grigsby-Grunow alone hit 4,000 sets/day (~1.2M/yr) in 1929; 1929 trade forecast was '5,000,000 or more' annual set sales feeding 13M sets in use, while actual 1929 US sales were 4.438M units and fell to 3.827M (1930), 3.420M (1931). Aggregate manufacturer capital invested ~$150M (Electronics, 1932) against a set-revenue pool that collapsed from $843M (1929) to $212M (1931). First-wave overshoot already visible 1925: Freed-Eisemann overstocked, selling below cost to Gimbels, laid off 1,200 by 1925; industry equipment revenue fell 16% in 1927 ($506M→$426M) on battery→AC-set transition glut.

equity_outcomes.name: RCA
equity_outcomes.outcome: $1.50-5.83 (1921) to $420 (1928); 5:1 split Mar 1929; peak $114.75 Sept 1929 (=$549-574 pre-split), P/E 72-73x; trough $2.625 May 1932 (-98%). Never paid a dividend during the entire boom (first common dividend 1937). Survived operationally, kept patent-toll + NBC franchise; stock took ~30 years to regain nominal 1929 peak

equity_outcomes.name: Kolster Radio Corp
equity_outcomes.outcome: Pure-capacity set maker: stock $10 (1927) to $95 (1928-29) to under $1 by 1930; receivership/bankruptcy 1930

equity_outcomes.name: Grigsby-Grunow (Majestic)
equity_outcomes.outcome: #2 maker 1928, #1 unit volume 1929 (4,000 sets/day, trainload shipments); reorganized 1933, bankrupt/liquidated 1934. Scale without IP moat

equity_outcomes.name: Atwater Kent (private)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Largest US set maker 1925 (12,000 employees); six years of declining sales after 1929; owner shut the company in 1936 rather than compete in midget-set price war

equity_outcomes.name: Freed-Eisemann
equity_outcomes.outcome: Early leader 1923-24; overstocked and undercapitalized by end-1924; selling below cost by 1925; laid off 1,200; effectively gone by late 1920s

equity_outcomes.name: Philco
equity_outcomes.outcome: Late entrant (1928, from battery-making) with cost/scale strategy; #1 by 1930; 977,000 sets and ~$34M sales in 1931, one of the few profitable makers that year. Survivor via low-cost + licensed IP

equity_outcomes.name: Zenith / Crosley / Emerson
equity_outcomes.outcome: Survived shakeout; Zenith ran losses 1930-33; Emerson rode the midget-radio segment ($20-35 sets). Survivors = cost leaders or niche innovators, all paying RCA toll

key_numbers: Radio equipment retail sales $M: 1922:60, 1923:136, 1924:358, 1925:430, 1926:506, 1927:426 (-16% mid-boom glut), 1928:651, 1929:843 (peak), 1931 sets-only:212, 1931 all-products:309 (Electronics 3/1932, primary)

Set units sold (US): 1929: 4,438,000 (4.2M consoles/midgets + 238k phono combos); 1930: 3,827,000; 1931: 3,420,000 (+471,659 exports); 1933: 3,600,000 — units fell only 23% peak-to-1931 while dollars fell 75%
Average set price: >$200 (1924), $35 low-end by 1927, $136-190 avg 1929 (console era), ~$62 avg 1931, midgets $20-57.50 in 1931-33 — ASP deflation -54% in 2 years post-peak
Manufacturer count: 600-1,200 assemblers mid-1920s -> ~155 (licensed+unlicensed) early 1932 -> 18 by 1934; ~97-98% cumulative attrition

RCA: revenue first 3 years of set sales (1922-24) $83.5M; earnings $2.5M (1925) -> $20M (1928) = 8x in 3 yrs; stock 94x from 1921 to Sept-1929 peak; P/E 72x; -98% to May 1932; zero dividends throughout boom

Patent toll: 7.5% royalty on licensee set sales (package license, ~25 licensees early 1920s), cut to 5% after 1930 antitrust suit / Nov 1932 consent decree (GE, Westinghouse, AT&T divested RCA stakes 1932)
Broadcast stations: 5 (1921) -> 556 (1923) = 112x in 2 yrs -> plateau ~530-680 through 1940 (station buildout saturated in 3 years)
Radio households: ~0.2% (1922) -> 10M+ (1927) -> 12.08M homes = 40.3% penetration (April 1930 census) -> 16.5M (March 1932) -> 60% (1934) -> 80% (1939): adoption S-curve never paused during the bust

Speculative financing: Meehan RCA pool Mar 9-30 1929, 68 participants, $12.6M capital, drove RCA $93->$109.75, ~$5M profit in ~10 trading days; NYSE broker call loans ~$3.5B end-1927 -> ~$8.5B Oct 1929; call money to ~20% Mar 1929; Fed discount rate to 6% Aug 1929
Radio advertising revenue $M (demand side kept growing through the bust): 1927:4.8, 1929:26.8, 1930:40.5, 1932:61.9, 1935:112.6, 1940:215.6
Industry totals 1931 (primary, Electronics 3/1932): 53.5M tubes ($69.55M), total products $309.27M, manufacturer investment ~$150M, ~100,000 peak employees
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: 1922-24: sets >$200 with waiting lists, assembler gross margins fat enough to pull in 600+ entrants in ~30 months. Equity signal: RCA at 72-73x earnings Sept 1929 after 8x earnings growth in 3 years; Kolster 9.5x stock move in 2 years on no durable economics. By 1925 the price signal had already inverted for first-wave assemblers (below-cost selling), while the market kept capitalizing the boom for 4 more years.
episodes.glut_depth: Industry set revenue -75% peak-to-1931 ($843M->$212M), roughly -80% to 1932-33 trough; units only -23% (1929->1931) — the glut expressed itself through price, not volume. Firm count -97-98% (600+->18 by 1934). Mid-boom mini-glut 1927: revenue -16% Y/Y from battery-set obsolescence inventory overhang. RCA equity -98%; sector speculative names -99% to -100%.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Demand was fully realized — and then some — but at collapsed prices. 1929 promoters projected 5M+ sets/yr; actual 1929-33 ran 3.4-4.4M/yr, i.e., ~70-90% of promise in units. Penetration went 0.2%->40% in 8 years and kept climbing to 60% (1934), 80% (1939) straight through the Depression; radio listening INCREASED during the bust (cheapest entertainment), and ad revenue rose every year except 1933. The bust destroyed producers' revenue/margins via 54% ASP deflation and 97% firm attrition, not via demand shortfall. Classic case: the technology over-delivered on adoption while under-delivering on producer economics.
episodes.financing_structure: Real-economy capex was mostly equity/internal: RCA self-financed from set profits and paid no dividend 1919-1937; the 1925-29 set-maker wave floated stock in the bull market (Kolster, Grigsby-Grunow, Fada etc.) — cheap equity, not bank debt, funded the entrant flood; assembly required little fixed capital (total manufacturer investment only ~$150M vs $843M peak annual revenue, capital turns >5x, which is why entry was so fast). The FINANCIAL boom was credit-fueled: broker call loans $3.5B (end-1927)->$8.5B (Oct 1929), call money ~20% (Mar 1929), organized pools (Meehan's RCA pool). Credit tightening (Fed 5%->6% Aug 1929, call-money squeeze) ended the equity mania with a ~2-month lag, and post-crash contraction of consumer installment credit crushed big-ticket console demand (shift to $20-60 cash-purchase midgets). BUT: the first industry shakeout (1925-27) happened in EASY credit — it was pure supply-response/price competition. Credit ended the stock bubble; competition had already ended the operating rents.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS (toll/IP/franchise): RCA — patent-pool toll of 7.5% (later 5%) on every licensed competitor's revenue, ~2,000 patents, plus NBC broadcast franchise; earned royalties through the Depression, survived -98% stock drawdown, rents only clipped by antitrust (1930 suit, Nov 1932 consent decree, GE/Westinghouse divestiture) — i.e., regulators, not entrants, ended the toll's exclusivity. AT&T kept transmission-equipment and network-wire rents ($2M/yr wire fees from NBC alone in 1929). CBS/NBC network franchises compounded (ad revenue 1927 $4.8M -> 1940 $215.6M). COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity): every large non-IP set maker — Atwater Kent (#1 in 1925, dead 1936), Grigsby-Grunow (#1 units 1929, bankrupt 1934), Kolster (bankrupt 1930), Freed-Eisemann (below-cost by 1925), plus ~580+ smaller assemblers. Survivors among makers (Philco, Zenith, Crosley, Emerson) survived on cost leadership/segment agility, thin margins — all while paying the RCA toll. Rule confirmed: assembly capacity earned ~3 years of rents; the IP chokepoint earned 11+ years (1921-1932 undiminished; royalties continued at 5% after) and was terminated politically, not competitively.
lessons_for_model: Scarcity-rent duration for pure-capacity/assembly players: 3 years (1922-25); entry lag ~12-30 months from margin signal to margin-destroying capacity; use entrant-flow gain high enough to produce 30-65x firm-count overshoot when entry barriers are near zero and capital turns >5x

Toll/IP rent duration: >=11 years at full rate (7.5% of downstream revenue 1921-1932), decay via regulatory hazard not supply response — model as annual antitrust/expropriation hazard ~5-10%/yr that clips the toll rate ~33% per event (7.5%->5%), rather than as competitive erosion

Two-wave structure: product-generation transition mid-boom (battery->AC sets) caused a -16% revenue air-pocket in 1927 two years before the terminal bust — include an obsolescence shock module with ~4-5 yr product-cycle period that can trigger inventory gluts independent of macro

Decouple units from dollars in the bust: calibrate demand so units fall only ~20-25% while ASP falls ~55% in 24 months and revenue falls ~75% over 3 years; adoption S-curve (0.2%->40% penetration in 8 yrs) continues THROUGH the financial bust
Bust lag: peak industry revenue to trough = 3 years (1929->1932/33); peak equity to trough = 2.7 years (Sept 1929 -> May 1932); first-wave capex peak (1925) to first shakeout = ~2 years

Leader equity path template for the AI analogue: ~90-100x over 8 years, terminal P/E ~72x, drawdown -98%, ~30 years to nominal recovery, company survives and keeps franchise — separate 'company survives' from 'equity holder survives'

Financing regime switch: real capex equity/internally financed (boom does NOT require bank leverage when capital turns are high); credit tightening (policy rate +100bp to 6%, call money 20%, broker loans +143% in 22 months then margin calls) ends the VALUATION boom with ~2-month lag; consumer-credit contraction transmits to durable demand with 6-12 month lag and forces down-market product mix

Survivorship calibration: P(survival|top-3 unit share, no IP) ~ 0.3 or less (Atwater Kent, Grigsby-Grunow died; only late-entrant cost-leader Philco lived); P(survival|toll position) ~ 1.0 operationally; apply this to distinguish NVDA/TSMC/ASML-type toll holders from neocloud/assembler-type capacity holders in the 2026-2036 run

Complement-side revenue (broadcasting/advertising = the 'application layer') grew every year through the bust except one (1933 dip) — model application-layer demand as nearly bust-immune while hardware-layer margins carry all the cyclical damage

Aggregate calibration anchors: firm attrition 97-98% over ~9 years; industry capital base (~$150M) small vs peak revenue ($843M) implies overshoot shows up as ENTRANT COUNT and price war, not stranded fixed assets — for capital-heavy AI datacenters, expect the same revenue math but with stranded-asset amplification the radio episode did NOT have

episodes.episode: US automobile industry boom-shakeout-bust: mass-motorization capex cycle, 253+ automakers to Big Three oligopoly, dealer/installment-credit channel, 1929 peak and Depression collapse
episodes.period: 1908-1933 (rents 1908-1921; saturation 1925-27; peak 1929; trough 1932-33; full recovery of unit volume not until 1949)
episodes.bottleneck: Mass-production capability itself: capital-intensive assembly-line plants (Highland Park 1910, moving line 1913, River Rouge ~$268M), machine tools, and process know-how. Anyone who could actually BUILD cars at volume earned rents in a seller's market 1908-1920 — demand (65k units 1908 → 1.9M 1920) outran installed capacity. Distribution was capital-light for manufacturers: franchised dealers paid cash on delivery and posted advance deposits, suppliers gave 30-90 day terms, so automakers ran on negative working capital, which turbocharged entry (253 firms by 1908) and later the supply response.
episodes.capex_overshoot: 1929 industry capacity ~6.5-8M units/yr vs peak sales of 5.3M cars (5.6M incl. trucks) = capacity ~1.3-1.5x peak demand at the top. But peak demand itself was credit-inflated and pull-forward: sustainable replacement-era demand proved ~3-3.5M (1934-37 recovery plateau), so capacity was ~2x demand-consistent volume. At the 1932 trough (1.3M units) utilization was ~18-25%. Earlier mini-cycle: 1918-20 capacity buildout vs 1921 sales of 1.5M produced the 1920-21 inventory crisis (Ford sat on ~$88M of inventory/parts; GM Q4-1920 sales 43,532 vs 106,946 a year earlier, -59%).

equity_outcomes.name: Ford (private)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Archetypal rent-winner then rent-loser: ~$28k founding capital (1903) supported dividends+buyout valuing firm ~$250M+ by 1919 (Dodge brothers' $10k stake returned ~$35M incl. dividends, ~3,500x). Net income $3M 1909, $25M 1914, $60M 1916, ~$75M 1921 at 55-57% unit share. Refused product differentiation; share fell to ~15% by 1927, Model T changeover shutdown (May 1927) cost ~$100M+, lost ~$120M cumulatively 1931-33. Survived on fortress balance sheet (no debt), never regained leadership.

equity_outcomes.name: General Motors
equity_outcomes.outcome: The moat-builder: near-bankrupt 1920 (Durant margin-debt blowup, DuPont/bankers bailout, Sloan installed). Built durable rents on differentiation (price ladder, annual model change), captive finance toll (GMAC, 1919), and dealer network. Share 12% (1921) to 32% (1929) to ~45% (1941). Net income $248M on ~$1.5B revenue 1929 (~16% margin); PROFITABLE AND DIVIDEND-PAYING EVERY DEPRESSION YEAR. Stock still fell $73 to $8.

equity_outcomes.name: Studebaker
equity_outcomes.outcome: Mid-scale generalist: receivership March 1933 (president Erskine ousted, suicide July 1933); reorganized, limped on, died 1963-66.

equity_outcomes.name: Durant Motors
equity_outcomes.outcome: Pure-capacity me-too entrant (founded 1921 on hype of Durant's name): bankruptcy filed Jan 30 1932, liquidated 1933. Total loss.

equity_outcomes.name: Willys-Overland
equity_outcomes.outcome: No. 2 producer in 1918; receivership 1933; survived only via WWII Jeep contract (a new government toll).

equity_outcomes.name: Luxury/commodity independents (Pierce-Arrow, Stutz, Marmon, Peerless, Franklin, Auburn-Cord-Duesenberg, Locomobile)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Essentially all -100%: dead 1929-1938. Undifferentiated volume also-rans (Moon, Kissel, Jordan, Gardner, Chandler) dead 1929-1932.

equity_outcomes.name: Chrysler
equity_outcomes.outcome: Late consolidator counterexample: formed 1925 from Maxwell wreckage, bought Dodge 1928 (leveraged), launched Plymouth 1928; passed Ford to #2 in 1930s. Entry via engineering IP + acquired dealer network, not greenfield capacity.

equity_outcomes.name: Hudson / Nash / Packard
equity_outcomes.outcome: Survived the 1930s shrunken (Nash via cash hoard, Packard by down-market move), but rents never returned; all gone by 1954-58 merger wave.

episodes.financing_structure: Manufacturers: overwhelmingly internal cash + float. Dealers paid cash/sight-draft on delivery and suppliers extended trade credit, so growth was self-financing (Ford expanded 1908-1927 with essentially zero long-term debt; refused bankers in the 1921 crisis and instead force-shipped inventory to dealers, making DEALERS borrow locally — the channel absorbed the credit shock). GM was the exception: external equity (DuPont ~$50M 1917-20, banker syndicates), and Durant personally blew up on ~$90M of margin debt in 1920. Demand side: installment credit was the boom's demand accelerant — GMAC founded 1919 (dealer floor-plan + consumer paper); by 1925-26 ~65-75% of cars sold on installments; down payments competed from 40-50% to as low as 10%. Credit's role in ending the boom: (1) 1920-21 — yes, directly: Fed discount rate to 7%, commodity/inventory deflation, killed ~100 makers and nearly GM; (2) 1929-32 — the boom was already dead from SATURATION (replacement demand exceeded new-buyer demand by 1927; registrations 23M = 1 vehicle per ~5-6 people); the 1928-29 Fed tightening and post-crash collapse of consumer credit and wealth then turned a plateau into a -76% volume crash. So: saturation killed the rents; credit contraction determined bust depth and timing, not the peak.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Promised/extrapolated: perpetual first-buyer growth ("a car for every family" and second cars). Realized: unit sales 181k (1910) → 1.9M (1920) → 3.6-4.0M (1923) → 5.3M (1929), i.e. the demand thesis was TRUE — ~23%/yr volume CAGR for two decades — yet still destroyed 95%+ of entrants. First-purchase demand saturated by 1925-27; the 1927-29 leg was replacement + credit pull-forward (down payments to 10%). Post-bust demand-consistent run-rate: 1.3M (1932), ~3.5M (1936-37); 1929's 5.3M not seen again until 1949. Being right about demand did not protect capacity owners.
episodes.glut_depth: Production -76% peak-to-trough (5.3M 1929 → 1.3M 1932) in 3 years; capacity utilization ~20% at trough; industry pricing wars, 44 makers (1929) → ~12 (1939); recovery to prior peak took 20 years (1949). In the 1920-21 mini-glut: GM quarterly sales -59% YoY, Ford dealer-channel stuffed with ~$88M inventory, car prices cut 20-30% overnight (Ford Model T cut from $575 to $440, Sep 1920).
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Peak scarcity-rent signals: Ford gross profit ~$220/car in 1909 (~25% of an $850 price); Ford net income $60M on ~500k units in 1916 (~$120/car, ~27% net margin); Ford ROE effectively infinite on $28k paid-in capital; 1921 net ~$75M at 55% share. GM 1929: $248M net, ~16.5% margin, ~30%+ ROE. Price signal of competition arriving: Model T price $850 (1908) → $440 (1920) → $265-290 (1924-25), i.e. -70% nominal / ~-80% real; per-unit profit for commodity segment approached zero by 1926 (Ford's base Runabout was sold BELOW factory cost in 1921 as a loss leader).
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS (moat/IP/toll): GM — segmentation + annual model change (planned obsolescence as engineered demand), captive credit toll (GMAC skimmed the financing spread on ~3/4 of its sales), franchised dealer lock-in, Fisher Body integration; profitable every year of the Depression. Chrysler — engineering IP and acquired distribution. Suppliers/toll-takers adjacent to the fight generally beat assemblers (component makers, GMAC, DuPont's GM stake). COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity): everyone whose only asset was the ability to assemble cars — 240+ firms 1908-1929, then 30+ more 1929-1939. Ford is the hinge case: world-best capacity + vertical integration but no differentiation moat; kept scale and survived, lost ALL excess margin (from 27% net margins to losses within a decade of peak share). Lesson: cost leadership in a standardizing product is a wasting asset; the durable rents accrued to demand-shaping (brand/segmentation), financing tolls, and distribution control — not to owning the most/best plants.
key_numbers: Firm count: ~253 active makers 1908 → 108 by 1923 → 44 by 1929 → ~12 by 1939; Big Three = ~80% of output 1929, 90% by 1939
Output: 65k units (1908) → 1.9M (1920) → 5.3M cars / 5.6M total (1929): ~23%/yr CAGR over 21 years
Model T price: $850 (1908) → $440 (Sept 1920 cut from $575) → $265-290 (1924-25); real price decline ~80%
Ford net income: $3M (1909), $25M (1914), $60M on 500k units (1916), ~$75M (1921, 55% unit share); paid-in capital $28k (1903)
GM 1929: net $248M, ~32% US share; GM stock $73 → $8 (-89%) 1929-32 while remaining profitable throughout
Installment credit: GMAC founded 1919; ~65-75% of cars sold on credit by 1925-26; down payments 40-50% → 10%
Saturation marker: by 1927 replacement demand > (first-time + additional-car) demand; 23M registrations, ~1 vehicle per 5-6 Americans by 1929
1920-21 shock: Fed discount rate 7%; GM Q4-1920 deliveries -59% YoY; Durant lost $90M margin position; Ford carried ~$88M excess inventory and pushed it onto dealers
Bust: 5.3M (1929) → 3.4M (1930) → 1.3M (1932), -76% in 3 years; utilization ~20%; 1929 volume not re-attained until 1949
Corporate deaths post-peak: Durant Motors bankrupt Jan 1932; Studebaker and Willys-Overland receivership 1933; Pierce-Arrow, Stutz, Marmon, Peerless, Franklin, Auburn-Cord all dead by 1938
lessons_for_model: Scarcity-rent duration ~13 years (1908-1921) for the ability-to-produce bottleneck; extend to ~17-19 years (to 1925-27) only for scale leaders. Model: rents decay once cumulative industry capacity crosses ~1x current demand, with margin half-life ~4-5 years after the first serious demand pause (1920-21).

Supply-response delay: 2-4 years from price/margin signal to new capacity online (plant build 1-2 yrs + ramp); entry lag near zero early (capital-light entry via supplier credit + dealer deposits — analogous to today's vendor-financed GPU clouds). Calibrate entry flow to margins with ~2yr lag and near-frictionless entry when the channel finances working capital.

Capex-momentum overshoot ratio: capacity/peak-demand ~1.3-1.5x at cycle top, capacity/sustainable-demand ~2x. Bust lag: ~3 years peak-capex(1926-29)-to-trough(1932); mini-cycle version: ~1 year (1920→1921).

Demand can grow 20%+/yr for 20 years, exactly as the bulls promised, and still bankrupt >95% of capacity owners: model firm-level ruin as driven by margin compression + shakeout, decoupled from aggregate demand realization.

Two distinct credit loops: (a) supply-side trade-credit/channel-stuffing loop — inventory shock propagates to dealers/suppliers within 2 quarters (1920-21); (b) demand-side installment loop — credit penetration 0→70% in ~7 years pulls forward ~1-2 years of demand and steepens the eventual bust by ~2x (sales fell 76% vs GDP -26%). Credit tightening (1920, 1929-32) sets bust TIMING/DEPTH; saturation sets the PEAK.

Rent-keeper taxonomy for terminal-state calibration: differentiation+finance-toll incumbent (GM) keeps ~15% net margins and positive earnings through the bust; scale/cost leader without moat (Ford) keeps volume share but margins go to ~0 within 6-8 years of peak; pure-capacity entrants go to -100%. Even the best moat's EQUITY draws down ~85-90% in the bust — separate cash-flow rents from market-price outcomes in the model.
Shakeout attrition rate: ~10%/yr net firm exit over 21 boom years even WHILE demand compounds 23%/yr; exit accelerates to ~12-15%/yr in the 1929-39 decade.
Utilization trajectory to reproduce: ~85-95% (1908-1919 seller's market) → ~70-80% at 1929 peak → ~20% at trough(+3yrs) → 20-year climb back to prior peak volume.

Price trajectory: real unit price -8 to -10%/yr for ~17 years once the dominant design (Model T/assembly line) standardizes; profit-per-unit for the commodity segment hits zero ~5 years before the aggregate volume peak (1926 vs 1929) — margins lead volumes as the bust predictor.
Consolidation endpoint: 3 firms / 80-90% share within ~15 years of margin peak; the consolidators (GM 1918-20, Chrysler 1925-28) buy distressed capacity/IP in the two credit crunches, not at the top.

episodes.episode: WWII US industrial mobilization and demobilization (the "unconstrained supply response" bound case): ships, aircraft, synthetic rubber, aluminum, machine tools
episodes.bottleneck: Physical production capacity itself: shipways, airframe plants, aluminum smelting/alumina, butadiene+styrene (synthetic rubber), and machine tools (the supplier-of-suppliers). Pre-1942 the binding constraint rotated: machine tools (1940-41) -> aluminum (1941-42) -> rubber (1942-43) -> manpower (1944). Owners of scarce capacity earned rents only briefly because the state deliberately capped them (excess profits tax + renegotiation) while simultaneously funding the supply response on its own balance sheet.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Massive but state-absorbed. Total new manufacturing facilities 1940-45: ~$25B (vs total 1939 US manufacturing structures+equipment stock ~$40B), ~2/3 government-financed; DPC alone $9.2B / 2,300 plants = ~2/3 of ALL new industrial capacity added. Peak capacity vs demand-consistent (1946-47) capacity: aircraft ~70x (96,318 planes built 1944 vs 1,330 military aircraft 1946; industry sales $16B 1944 -> $1.2B 1947); merchant shipbuilding ~20-50x (19.2M DWT delivered 1943 vs near-zero US commercial orders for 15+ yrs; 2,277 ships mothballed in reserve fleet by 1950); machine tools ~3-4x (peak rate 365k/yr Aug 1942; 300k surplus units dumped on postwar market vs normal absorption ~30-50k/yr); aluminum ~2x (163kt 1939 -> 920kt 1943 primary; roughly half of capacity idled 1945-46). Counterexample: synthetic rubber capacity (~900kt/yr, 51 plants, $700M) was fully grown into by early 1950s — general-purpose/fungible capacity retained value, specialized assembly capacity went to scrap.

equity_outcomes.name: Aircraft primes as a group (Douglas, Curtiss-Wright, North American, etc.)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Industry sales -92.5% ($16B 1944 -> $1.2B 1947). Notably, aviation shares traded at 3-5x earnings DURING peak production — the market priced the postwar bust in advance, so wartime volume never translated into wartime market cap. Pure-assembly capacity was worthless on V-J Day.

equity_outcomes.name: Curtiss-Wright
equity_outcomes.outcome: No.2 US war contractor by volume; hoarded cash, skipped jet R&D; revenue collapsed >90%, lost airframe business permanently. Textbook capacity-without-IP casualty.

equity_outcomes.name: Boeing
equity_outcomes.outcome: Sales fell from ~$421M (1944) to ~$14M (1946), near-death; survived on IP acquired via war R&D (swept-wing data, large-jet know-how) -> B-47/B-52/707. Long-run rent keeper via technology moat, not wartime capacity.

equity_outcomes.name: Kaiser shipbuilding / Kaiser-Frazer
equity_outcomes.outcome: Built ~1,490 ships, exited shipbuilding entirely by 1946 (Richmond, Portland yards closed; Marinship closed May 1946). Kaiser-Frazer autos (bought Willow Run) burned >$100M and failed by 1953. Capacity player competed away.

equity_outcomes.name: Kaiser Aluminum + Reynolds Metals
equity_outcomes.outcome: The big winners: bought government aluminum plants (Spokane, Tacoma, Trentwood, Troutdale) at deep discounts to cost 1946-49; rode postwar aluminum demand. Bought the glut instead of building the boom.

equity_outcomes.name: Alcoa
equity_outcomes.outcome: Held ~90% of US primary capacity 1939; government sale of surplus plants to Kaiser/Reynolds cut it to 33% of North American capacity by 1956. Monopoly rents destroyed by recycled overcapacity, not by the boom itself.

equity_outcomes.name: Higgins Industries
equity_outcomes.outcome: Landing-craft champion, ~20,000 employees at peak; contracts cancelled, shrank to <1,000, effectively gone by late 1940s.

equity_outcomes.name: Machine-tool industry
equity_outcomes.outcome: Output peaked Aug 1942, fell >50% by 1944 while the war was still on (orders saturated); 300k surplus machines at ~15-30c/$ crushed new-tool demand until Korea (1950). Supplier-of-suppliers busts first.

episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Rents were policy-capped, not market-cleared: excess profits tax 95% statutory (85.5% net of postwar credit) from Oct 1940; Renegotiation Act (Apr 1942) clawed back $11B of "excessive" profits on ~$200B of contracts (~5.5% of contract value deemed excess and recaptured). Corporate after-tax profits still rose ~70% 1940-44 ($6.4B->~$10.8B) on 2x sales — i.e., after all caps, net margins actually COMPRESSED during the boom. Cost-plus-fixed-fee ran at 4-7% fees. The genuine scarcity-rent window was mid-1940 to early 1942 (before EPT bite + renegotiation), when defense-order backlogs tripled valuations of machine-tool and airframe firms.
episodes.glut_depth: $90B (cost basis) of surplus war property at V-J Day; War Assets Administration sold ~$34B of it 1946-49 at roughly 15-20 cents on the dollar overall. ~68,000 aircraft scrapped/smelted for ingot; ~300,000 surplus machine tools dumped; 2,277 merchant ships mothballed (NDRF peak 1950) and Ship Sales Act 1946 exports depressed US commercial shipbuilding for ~20 years. Aluminum: ~50% of capacity idled 1945-46, resolved by selling plants to entrants. Rubber: no glut — demand grew into capacity; 26 plants sold 1955 for $285M, recovering 100% of remaining government investment (earlier sales 1946-50 had recovered >half of the $700M).
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Demand was 100% realized while policy willed it ($59B munitions output 1944 alone; cumulative war output ~$183B) and then cancelled ~overnight: contract terminations of ~$23-35B within weeks of V-J Day; real military spending fell from ~38% of GNP (1944-45) to 4.3% of GNP ($10B) by 1947. Real GNP fell ~12% 1945-46 (measured), but real PRIVATE GDP rose 29.5% in 1946 — pent-up civilian demand absorbed general-purpose capacity almost instantly; only specialized war capacity (airframes, shipways, ordnance) had no successor demand.
episodes.financing_structure: Almost no private credit in the boom: government financed ~2/3 of all new plant directly (DPC $9.2B GOCO leases + military construction), separating asset risk (state) from operating risk (contractor); firms explicitly refused to build specialized capacity on their own balance sheets, correctly anticipating postwar worthlessness. Private share funded from retained earnings + 5-year accelerated amortization certificates (write off war plant in 60 months). Working capital via guaranteed V-loans ($10B guaranteed). Macro funding: taxes (~45%) + war bonds/Fed-pegged debt. CREDIT TIGHTENING PLAYED NO ROLE IN ENDING THE BOOM — demand cancellation did. The state was the equity sink for the entire capacity writedown.
key_numbers: Total new manufacturing facilities 1940-45: ~$25B; government-financed ~$17B (~2/3); DPC: $9.2B, 2,300 plants, ~2/3 of all new industrial capacity
Facility capex PEAKED in 1942 (WPB then throttled new plant starts); munitions OUTPUT peaked H2-1943/1944 at $59B/yr; bust Aug 1945 => peak-capex-to-bust lag ~3 yrs, peak-output-to-bust ~1 yr
Aircraft: 6,019 (1940) -> 96,318 (1944) = 16x units in 4 yrs (~50x airframe pounds); -> 1,330 military (1946) = 98.6% collapse in 18 months; industry sales $16B->$1.2B (1944->47)

Liberty ships: 2,710 built; avg build time ~250 days (early 1942) -> <50 days (late 1943); man-hours/ship 1.1M -> ~0.5M; labor productivity +40%/yr; unit-cost learning ~16-22% per cumulative doubling (~80-85% curve); total US merchant output 5,777 ships / 39M+ DWT
Synthetic rubber: 0 (1941) -> 22,434t (1942) -> 231,722t (1943) -> 753,111t (1944): 34x in 24 months, 51 plants, $700M, from lab-scale to world's largest industry in ~30 months
Aluminum: 163kt (1939) -> 920kt (1943) = 5.6x in 4 yrs; postwar Alcoa share 90% -> 33% (1956) after surplus plants sold to Kaiser/Reynolds
Machine tools: peak annual rate 365k units (Aug 1942), output halved by 1944 BEFORE war ended; 300k surplus units dumped postwar; sector depressed until Korea 1950
Rent suppression: EPT 95% statutory/85.5% net (Oct 1940); Renegotiation Act Apr 1942 recaptured $11B on ~$200B contracts; scarcity-rent window mid-1940 to early-1942 ~= 2 years
Bust: contract cancellations $23-35B within weeks of V-J Day; military spend 38% GNP -> 4.3% GNP (1947); real GNP -12% (1946) but real private GDP +29.5% (1946)
Glut disposal: $90B surplus at cost; WAA sold $34B at ~15-20c/$; 68k aircraft scrapped; 2,277 ships mothballed; rubber plants the exception - sold 1955 at 100% of remaining book ($285M for 26 plants)
Decision-to-output pipeline delay: 12-24 months for greenfield plants (Willow Run ground-broken Apr 1941, rated output mid-1943, peak 1944 - 3 yrs to full rate)
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS: (a) IP/technology holders — Boeing (jet/swept-wing know-how from war R&D), petroleum/chemical majors (catalytic cracking, butadiene, styrene process knowledge kept after plants sold), electronics/radar firms (RCA, Raytheon -> postwar TV/microwave); (b) glut buyers — Kaiser Aluminum and Reynolds bought state-built smelters at cents on the dollar and captured the postwar aluminum century; airlines bought $90k surplus C-54s/DC-3s and ran them profitably for a decade; (c) brand/distribution incumbents (GM, Ford) reconverting into pent-up consumer demand. COMPETED AWAY / DEAD: pure capacity operators — Curtiss-Wright (volume champion, no jet IP), Kaiser and Higgins shipbuilding, Marinship, emergency shipyards (virtually all closed 1945-46), machine-tool makers (their own surplus output cannibalized them), Willow Run/Kaiser-Frazer. Incumbent monopolist Alcoa lost its rents not to the boom but to the recycled glut. Rule confirmed: capacity rents die with the shortage; process-knowledge, technology, and cheaply-acquired distressed assets are the only durable rents.
lessons_for_model: UPPER BOUND for supply-response loop gain when capital is unconstrained: sector output 5-35x in 24-48 months (rubber 34x/24mo, aircraft 16x units/48mo, aluminum 5.6x/48mo). Calibrate AI-datacenter/robotics max capacity growth <= these; anything faster than ~3x/yr sustained is outside the WWII envelope even with state-level will

Pipeline delay (decision -> first output): 12-24 months; (decision -> full rated output): 30-40 months. Use 1.5-3 yr capacity-construction delay in the stock-flow model — this delay, not capital availability, set the mobilization speed

Learning-curve parameter: 16-22% unit-cost decline per cumulative doubling (80-85% curve) for repetitive complex manufacture; labor productivity +40%/yr for ~3 yrs then plateau. Apply to robot/server assembly, not to chips (different regime)
Scarcity-rent duration ~2 years when supply response is maximal AND rents are policy-capped; model should produce 2-4 yrs for market-driven analogs. Margin peak precedes output peak by ~2 yrs

Supplier-of-suppliers (machine tools ~ today's semicap/optics) peaks FIRST and busts ~2 years before final demand does: orders saturate once downstream capacity is built. Model semicap/networking capex as leading the datacenter cycle by 18-30 months with a >50% drawdown while end demand still grows

Peak-capex-to-bust lag: ~3 yrs; peak-output-to-90%-collapse: 12-18 months when demand is a single deep-pocket buyer that revises (state then, hyperscalers now). Concentrated-buyer demand can cancel ~instantly - model demand-revision shock as step function, not gradual

Financing regime determines the terminator: WWII boom was state/internal-cash financed => NO credit-discipline loop fired; boom ended by demand cancellation. 2026 analog: hyperscaler internal cash flow (~70% of AI capex) => credit tightening will NOT end the core boom; it only kills the levered fringe (neoclouds = the merchant shipyards). Set credit-loop gain low for funders with >$50B FCF, high for debt-financed capacity resellers

Glut resolution pricing: surplus specialized capacity clears at 15-30 cents on the dollar and suppresses NEW capex in that sector for 10-20 years (shipbuilding 2 decades, machine tools 5 yrs). Model post-bust GPU/robot secondary-market price at 15-30% of cost and let it gate new-build for 5+ yrs

Fungibility spread: general-purpose capacity (rubber=commodity chemical; analog: power, shells of datacenters, standard robots) gets fully absorbed by successor demand within 5-8 yrs and recovers ~100% of book; specialized capacity (airframe lines; analog: single-tenant AI campuses, custom ASIC lines) recovers ~15%. Carry two salvage-value parameters, not one

Rent keepers are IP/process-knowledge holders and distressed-asset buyers, never capacity operators: in the model, assign durable (10yr+) rents only to nodes with technology moats (chip design, foundry process, models w/ distribution) and to post-bust acquirers; capacity-node rents must mean-revert to cost-of-capital within 2-4 yrs of supply response onset

Equity anticipates: wartime aircraft stocks traded at 3-5x peak earnings — the market discounts the bust ~3 yrs before it arrives once overshoot is visible. Model equity multiples compressing while fundamentals still improve (already visible in 2025-26 semicap/power multiples?)

Incumbent-share destruction via recycled glut: dominant supplier 90% -> 33% share within 10 yrs of bust because distressed assets seed competitors. NVDA-analog risk parameter: post-bust cheap-GPU secondary market seeding rivals/inference clouds

episodes.bottleneck: Leading-edge wafer fab capacity (clean-room + lithography). Fabs took 18-30 months from board approval to volume output and cost escalated ~2x per generation ($100M in 1980, ~$1B by 1995, ~$3-4B by 2008), so demand surges (PC waves, Windows 95, dot-com, netbooks) hit a fixed short-run supply curve and spot prices spiked far above cost. But the capacity itself was undifferentiated — any entrant with capital could buy the same equipment from AMAT/Nikon/ASML — so scarcity rents were structurally temporary. The only within-industry moats were process-node leadership (Samsung's 1-2 generation cost/bit lead of 20-30%) and, after 2013, oligopoly structure itself (3 survivors, $10-15B fab entry ticket).
episodes.capex_overshoot: 1995-96 peak: ~50 new fab construction plans announced in 1995-96 alone; semiconductor capex exceeded 30% of industry production value; DRAM-maker capex/revenue hit 50-80% (Korean chaebol near or above 100% in expansion years). Bit-supply growth ran ~70-80%/yr vs demand-consistent ~50-60%/yr, i.e. supply overshoot ratio ~1.3-1.6x. Result: 1995 DRAM revenue of ~$41.5B was not re-attained in nominal terms for ~18 years. 2000-01 repeat: DRAM sales $29-30B (2000) collapsed to ~$11B (2001), -62%, after capacity ordered in the 1999-2000 boom landed into the dot-com demand hole. 2006-07: Vista-anticipation capex (Qimonda, Elpida, Powerchip, ProMOS all expanding simultaneously) produced ~2x bit oversupply vs demand; prices fell 85% in 2007 before demand even rolled over.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Unit/bit demand almost always materialized — DRAM bit demand grew ~50-70%/yr for decades (PC waves, then mobile). The bust driver was price, not volume: supply elasticity destroyed revenue even as bits shipped grew. E.g. 2001: bits shipped kept growing while revenue fell 62% and per-chip prices fell ~90%. This is the canonical case of 'demand was real, rents still died' — directly analogous to AI compute: usage growth does not protect margins if capacity is commodity.
episodes.glut_depth: Prices repeatedly fell BELOW cash cost for 2-4 quarters at troughs: 256K DRAM $8.95 (Jan 1985) to $2.95 (Sep 1985), 64K to ~$0.30-0.75; per-megabit price >$3 (1995) to <$0.16 (1998), ~95% in 3 years (-51% in 1996, -65% in 1997); -90% in 2001 (128Mb SDRAM ~$18 mid-2000 to <$1 late 2001); -85% in 2007 then -58% in 2008, DDR2 1Gb broke through $1.00 cash cost Oct 2008 and traded ~$0.58-0.60, below bare materials cost. Industry-wide: Japanese DRAM makers lost ~$4B in 1985-86; global DRAM industry lost ~$12.5B in 2008 alone. Cumulative economic profit of the DRAM industry 1974-2012 was approximately zero.
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Boom-peak gross margins for leading suppliers exceeded 50-65% (1993-95 supercycle; again 1999-2000 and H2 2006). Spot prices at peaks ran 2-4x contract/cost. The 1993-95 boom was the longest rent window (~3 years) because it coincided with maximum fab lead times and pre-Korean-capacity arrival; most other rent windows lasted only 12-24 months before new supply landed.
episodes.financing_structure: Regime-dependent, and it determined who died, not when the boom ended. US firms (1970s-80s): internal cash flow + equity — hard budget constraints forced fast exits (Intel, Mostek, National, AMD, Motorola all out by 1985-86). Japanese (1980s): cheap keiretsu bank debt (cost of capital ~6% vs US ~12%) let them absorb ~$4B of 1985-86 losses and buy share — predatory endurance financed by credit. Korean (1990s): chaebol debt at 300-500% debt/equity; the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis credit crunch is the ONE episode where credit tightening directly forced restructuring (government-directed 'Big Deal': LG Semicon forced into Hyundai, 1999). Hynix 2001: ~$14B debt, creditors (largely state-owned banks) provided ~$7B bailout incl. $2B debt-equity swap and 8.6 trillion won restructuring — soft budget constraint that prolonged global overcapacity (US/EU imposed 44.7%/34.8% countervailing duties in 2003). Qimonda 2009: killed by credit denial during GFC — Infineon refused funding, Saxony state-aid talks failed; €1.2B FY2008 operating loss, insolvent 23 Jan 2009. Elpida: Japanese state bailout 2009 (~¥30B equity + ~¥100B guaranteed loans) bought 3 years; refinancing impossible in 2012, filed 27 Feb 2012 with ~¥448B (~$5.5B) liabilities — largest Japanese manufacturing bankruptcy to that date. NET: busts were initiated by endogenous supply overshoot (sometimes amplified by exogenous demand shock: 1985 PC slump, 2001 dot-com, 2008 GFC); credit tightening was the executioner of weak players and the accelerant of consolidation, not usually the boom-ender. State credit systematically lengthened gluts by keeping zombie capacity alive (Hynix 2001, Taiwan Memory 2009, Elpida 2009-12).

equity_outcomes.name: Intel (DRAM era)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Share of DRAM market 83% (1974) to 1.3% (1984); exited DRAM mid-1986 after ~$107-173M 1986 loss, closed 8 plants, cut 7,200 jobs (1/3 of company); pivot to x86 microprocessors (IP moat) created one of the great franchises — the escape-to-IP template

equity_outcomes.name: Micron
equity_outcomes.outcome: Serial near-death survivor: ~-80% (1995-96), -93% (2000-02, ~$97 to ~$6.60), ~-90% (2007-08, to $1.59 Nov 2008); survived on low-cost culture + buying distressed assets (TI's DRAM 1998, Toshiba's Dominion 2002, Elpida 2013 for $2.5B); +240% in 2013 once oligopoly formed

equity_outcomes.name: Qimonda
equity_outcomes.outcome: IPO Aug 2006 at $13 (below range); insolvent 23 Jan 2009; equity -100% in 2.5 years; world #2 DRAM maker by capacity destroyed by one down-cycle

equity_outcomes.name: Elpida (NEC+Hitachi JV, 1999)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Last Japanese DRAM maker; state-bailed 2009; bankrupt Feb 2012, ~$5.5B liabilities, shareholders wiped out; sold to Micron for $2.5B (~70% of Elpida's debts never repaid)

equity_outcomes.name: Hynix (ex-Hyundai Electronics)
equity_outcomes.outcome: ~-95% 2000-2002; $7B creditor bailout + massive debt-equity dilution 2001; survived as ward of Korean state banks; eventually SK acquisition (2012) and trillion-dollar-class winner post-consolidation — but original shareholders were nearly wiped

equity_outcomes.name: Samsung Electronics
equity_outcomes.outcome: Drawdowns of 60-80% in 1996-98 and 2000-01 but the structural winner: invested counter-cyclically into every trough (notably 1996-98 and 2008), kept fabs running flat-out in 2007-08 to bleed rivals below cash cost; DRAM share ~10% (1990) to ~18% (1995) to 30%+ (2005) to 40%+; gained roughly 3-6pp share per bust

equity_outcomes.name: Texas Instruments
equity_outcomes.outcome: Exited DRAM 1998 (sold fabs to Micron), redeployed into analog/DSP (IP-rich, sticky) — like Intel, escaping commodity capacity into differentiated IP was the winning equity move

episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: Kept durable rents: (1) firms that EXITED capacity into IP — Intel (x86), TI (analog/DSP); (2) Samsung via perpetual process-node lead (20-30% cost/bit advantage = only intra-commodity moat) plus balance-sheet depth to invest counter-cyclically; (3) post-2013, the surviving triopoly itself (Samsung ~45%, SK Hynix, Micron) — consolidation converted commodity capacity into a quasi-toll: 2017-18 DRAM operating margins hit 50-70%, something never sustained in the 20-supplier era. Competed away: every pure-capacity player without cost leadership or a sovereign backstop — Mostek, National, AMD, Motorola, Intel-as-DRAM (1985-86); all five Japanese majors (NEC, Hitachi, Fujitsu, Toshiba, Mitsubishi) exited 1999-2012 via Elpida's death; LG Semicon (1999); Qimonda (2009); Taiwanese fabs (Powerchip, ProMOS) reduced to foundry work post-2009. Supplier count: ~20 meaningful DRAM makers mid-1990s, mid-teens 2000s, 4 in 2012, 3 by 2014. Equipment suppliers (AMAT, ASML, TEL) captured a share of every boom's capex regardless of which memory maker won — the picks-and-shovels layer monetized the overshoot itself, though cyclically.
