lessons_for_model: Supply-response delay = 1.5-2.5 yrs (fab build time). Scarcity-rent window = delay + ~0.5 yr ordering hesitation: median ~2 yrs, range 1-3. Model should NOT produce commodity-capacity rents lasting >3 yrs while entry is uncapitalized-constrained only.

Capex-momentum loop gain: at peak margins (gross margin >50%), capex/revenue rises to 50-80% (2-3x sustainable ~20-25%); resulting bit-supply growth overshoots demand-consistent growth by 1.3-1.6x. Calibrate the overshoot ratio to ~1.4x central.

Bust lag: prices roll over 0.5-1.5 yrs after peak capex commitment (median ~1-1.5); capacity ordered AT the peak lands ~2 yrs later and extends the trough — model needs pipeline capacity (capex in transit) as an explicit stock so the bust deepens after prices have already crashed.

Price dynamics at bust: ASP -60% to -90% within 12-24 months; prices sit BELOW cash cost 2-4 quarters because high fixed cost + low marginal cost means nobody idles capacity voluntarily (Samsung ran flat-out in 2008 deliberately). Marginal-cost pricing floor, not average-cost, in glut states.

Demand realization is NOT the failure mode: bit demand grew 50-70%/yr through every bust. Calibrate so revenue/margin collapse occurs with demand fully realized — supply elasticity alone must be able to destroy rents (critical for AI-compute analogy).

Credit-discipline loop: credit tightening is the selector, not the trigger. Endogenous overshoot (+ occasional exogenous demand shock: 1985, 2001, 2008) triggers the bust; credit access then determines exit order. State/soft credit (Hynix 2001, Elpida 2009, Taiwan 2009) extends glut duration by 1-3 yrs by keeping zombie capacity alive — include a zombie-capacity stock gated on bailout propensity.

Attrition rate: each bust removes ~2-4 of the marginal suppliers; rents become durable ONLY when supplier count reaches ~3 (post-2013: operating margins 30-70% sustained). Model should show rent duration flipping from ~2 yrs to quasi-permanent once HHI crosses the oligopoly threshold — the moat is consolidation + capital barrier ($10-15B/fab), not the capacity itself.

Winner playbooks to reproduce: (a) escape-to-IP (Intel 1986, TI 1998) converts dying commodity position into durable differentiated rents; (b) counter-cyclical capex with cost/node lead (Samsung) gains 3-6pp share per bust and compounds; (c) distressed-asset acquisition at ~10-30 cents on the replacement dollar (Micron/Elpida $2.5B) is how laggards survive to the oligopoly endgame.

Equity calibration: pure-capacity players see -80% to -100% drawdowns EVERY cycle (Micron -93%, Qimonda/Elpida -100%); even the eventual winner (Samsung) draws down 60-80%. Long-run cumulative industry economic profit approximately 0 pre-consolidation — scarcity rents earned in booms are fully returned in busts unless structure changes.

Revenue high-water-mark rule: after a major overshoot, nominal peak revenue can take 10-18 yrs to re-attain (1995 peak to ~2013) even with volume growing 50%+/yr — price deflation (~30%/yr per-bit secular) swamps volume. For AI: token/compute price deflation can suppress revenue for a decade despite exploding usage.

episodes.episode: US/Global telecom & fiber-optic buildout boom-bust (post-Telecom Act 1996 through glut absorption)
episodes.period: 1996-2003 (boom 1996-2000, peak capex 2000-Q1 2001, bust 2001-2002, capex trough 2003, glut absorption ~2004-2015 on long-haul/submarine routes)
episodes.bottleneck: Long-haul bandwidth (lit fiber capacity) was the perceived scarce input for the exploding web, monetized as IRUs/leased circuits; scarcity narrative anchored on WorldCom/UUNET claim that internet traffic 'doubled every 100 days' (~1000%/yr). Actual backbone traffic (Odlyzko, AT&T data) doubled ~annually (~100%/yr) — a ~10x demand-growth misperception. Supply responded on two axes simultaneously: new fiber (80-90 million fiber-miles laid 1995-2001, ~5x long-haul route miles) AND DWDM technology multiplying capacity per existing fiber pair ~100x over 1996-2001. Bandwidth was a pure commodity with zero switching cost — no toll/moat once parallel routes existed.
episodes.capex_overshoot: US telecom carrier capex roughly doubled from ~$60B (1996) to ~$110-120B peak (2000), then fell ~60-70% to ~$40B by 2003. Total sector spend 1996-2001: >$500B US (much estimated $2T globally incl. wireless/licenses). Capacity vs demand: by 2001-02 only ~2.6-5% of installed fiber strands were lit (Merrill Lynch est. 2.6% of capacity in use; ~95-97% dark), and lit fiber itself ran well below full utilization — implied potential-capacity overshoot of ~20-50x demand-consistent levels on long-haul routes; route-level physical overshoot ~5-10x (multiple parallel builds on identical city pairs: WorldCom, Global Crossing, Level 3, Qwest, Williams, 360networks all built the same corridors). Root cause of overshoot ratio: 10x demand misperception x each of ~6 rivals building for 100% of projected market share.

equity_outcomes.name: Cisco Systems
equity_outcomes.outcome: Peak mkt cap $555B (Mar 2000, briefly world's most valuable co., ~130-200x earnings, ~30x revenue). Stock $79->$9.50 (2000-2002). $2.25B excess-inventory write-off Apr 2001. Revenue only dipped ($18.9B FY00 -> $22.3B FY01 -> $18.9B FY02) — the multiple, not the business, collapsed. Survived with router/switch moat intact; took 25 years (Dec 2025) to regain nominal price peak.

equity_outcomes.name: Corning
equity_outcomes.outcome: Stock ~$113 (Sep 2000) -> ~$1.10-1.50 (Jul-Oct 2002). Fiber demand evaporated; revenue fell to ~$4B; near-death but survived on glass/ceramics IP and later won FTTH + display glass. Fiber manufacturing IP durable, but rents took >10 years to return.

equity_outcomes.name: WorldCom
equity_outcomes.outcome: Chapter 11 Jul 21, 2002 — largest US bankruptcy ever at the time: $107B assets, ~$41B debt, $11B accounting fraud used to mask demand shortfall. Equity zeroed; peak mkt cap ~$186B (1999).

equity_outcomes.name: Global Crossing
equity_outcomes.outcome: Chapter 11 Jan 28, 2002 (4th-largest US bankruptcy): $22.4B assets, $12.4B debts, ~$25B total collapse. Peak mkt cap ~$47B (Feb 2000); spent ~$15B building network; 61.5% stake sold to ST Telemedia for $250M (~1-2 cents on the dollar for the assets).

equity_outcomes.name: JDS Uniphase
equity_outcomes.outcome: FY2001 net loss $56.1B (mostly goodwill write-offs from stock-funded acquisitions) — then the largest annual loss in corporate history. Stock ~$153 -> under $2.

equity_outcomes.name: Lucent
equity_outcomes.outcome: $84 (Dec 1999) -> $0.55 (Oct 2002). Vendor financing (~$8B commitments) to doomed CLECs boomeranged. Never recovered; absorbed by Alcatel 2006.

equity_outcomes.name: Nortel
equity_outcomes.outcome: Peak mkt cap ~C$398B (~35% of TSX, Jul 2000); C$124 -> under C$0.50 by Aug 2002. Limped on, bankrupt 2009.

equity_outcomes.name: Level 3
equity_outcomes.outcome: ~$132 (Mar 2000) -> ~$2.85 (Oct 2002). Survived only via emergency $500M convertible (Buffett/Longleaf, Jul 2002); became the consolidator that bought distressed fiber for cents on the dollar.

equity_outcomes.name: 360networks / PSINet / Winstar / NorthPoint / Exodus / Williams Comm / XO (CLEC-longhaul cohort)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Essentially all bankrupt 2001-2002; $110B of telecom bankruptcies in 18 months (~25% of all US corporate defaults in the window, 2x the S&L crisis price tag).

episodes.financing_structure: Overwhelmingly external, debt-heavy — the opposite of today's hyperscaler-cash-funded pattern. >$500B of US telecom bonds issued 1996-2001; >$1T total debt+equity raised by broadband/telecom sector since 1998 (Morgan Stanley), excluding bank loans, vendor financing, and receivables securitization; ~$1.6T all-in Wall Street financing commonly cited. Vendor financing from Lucent/Nortel/Cisco (~$15-25B) recycled equipment revenue into customer credit, corrupting the demand signal. CLECs and greenfield long-haul carriers were ~100% capital-market dependent with no operating cash flow. Credit tightening DID end the boom and did so abruptly: European 3G spectrum auctions (spring 2000, ~$100B+) first spooked lenders; telecom junk yields spiked; then the bond market slammed shut — 'in January 2001 a telecom could raise billions; by April 2001 it could not raise 5 cents' — and Moody's declared markets closed to the sector through 2002. Speculative-grade default rate rose 5.68% (2000) -> 8.57% (2001), telecoms = 18.5% of all 2001 defaults. The credit shutoff, not observed demand shortfall, was the proximate bust trigger; fraud (WorldCom's $11B, Qwest/Global Crossing hollow IRU swaps booking capacity trades as revenue) had masked the demand miss and bought the boom roughly one extra year.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Promised: traffic doubling every 100 days (~10x/yr), repeated by FCC chairs, Commerce Dept, VP Gore. Realized: ~2x/yr (Odlyzko) — real and sustained for a decade, but 10x slower than capacity was built for. Demand DID eventually fill the fiber (all dark fiber ultimately used, enabling YouTube/cloud/streaming), but only ~10-15 years later and at prices ~95-99% below boom-era projections, so the demand arrived without the revenue. Fake demand: capacity-swap round-tripping between carriers inflated apparent bandwidth revenue growth 1999-2001.
episodes.glut_depth: At trough (2002): ~2.6-5% of fiber strands lit, 95-97% dark. Transatlantic/long-haul lease prices fell >90% in 2-3 years (STM-1 transatlantic IRU ~$3M+ in 1999 -> low hundreds of $K by 2002-04), then continued falling ~20-40%/yr for a decade. Glut suppressed new long-haul construction for over a decade: after the last boom-era transatlantic cables (~2003), no new transatlantic cable entered service until ~2015 (Hibernia Express) — ~12 years of zero new supply needed. Long-haul wholesale bandwidth never regained pricing power; the scarcity rent was permanently competed to commodity cost-plus.
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Equipment layer: Cisco gross margins ~65% with ~30x price/sales and $555B cap at peak (Mar 2000); Corning bid from split-adjusted ~$10 to $113 in ~18 months on fiber scarcity narrative. Carrier layer: transatlantic STM-1 IRUs ~$3M+ (1999) with O&M $150K/yr; bandwidth treated as appreciating scarce asset (IRUs booked as assets and swapped). Price signal inverted fast: wholesale bandwidth prices were already falling 40-60%/yr on competitive routes by 1999-2000 even as capex was still accelerating — capex momentum overrode the visible price signal by ~1.5-2 years.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS (IP/moat/toll): Cisco — router/switch architecture + enterprise lock-in; multiple compressed 90% but franchise and 60%+ gross margins survived. Incumbent last-mile owners (Verizon/SBC/BellSouth) — the local-access physical toll was never overbuilt; they later bought the long-haul casualties (Verizon-MCI, SBC-AT&T, 2005) for pennies. Qualcomm-style IP royalties survived. Corning kept manufacturing IP but waited a decade for rents. COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity): every non-incumbent long-haul carrier — WorldCom, Global Crossing, 360networks, Williams, plus the whole CLEC cohort — because bandwidth is undifferentiated, buildable in parallel, and priced at marginal cost under glut. Vendors leveraged to those carriers (Lucent, Nortel) died with them despite having technology, killed by vendor-financing credit exposure and customer concentration. GLUT ARBITRAGEURS won biggest: Google et al. bought dark fiber at ~1-5 cents on the dollar; Level 3/ST Telemedia consolidated distressed assets. Rule confirmed: rents accrued to (a) un-overbuildable chokepoints (last mile), (b) design/IP layers, (c) buyers of distressed capacity — never to the capacity builders.
key_numbers: Telecom Act Feb 1996 = deregulation starting gun; boom duration to peak capex: ~4.5 years
US telecom capex: ~$60B (1996) -> ~$110-120B peak (2000) -> ~$40B (2003): +100% up-leg over 4 yrs, -65% down-leg over 3 yrs
>$500B spent on US networks 1996-2001; 80-90 million fiber-miles laid 1995-2001; ~$2T global sector spend incl. wireless
Claimed demand growth 10x/yr vs actual 2x/yr = 10x misperception, sustained ~4 years (1997-2000) against available contrary data
DWDM capacity-per-fiber multiplier ~100x over 1996-2001 (technology-driven supply shock on top of physical build)
Fiber utilization at trough: 2.6-5% lit (Merrill Lynch 2.6%, 2002); 95-97% dark
Bandwidth price path: -90%+ in 2-3 yrs (2000-2003), then -20-40%/yr for ~10 more yrs; STM-1 transatlantic ~$3M (1999) -> ~$0.2-0.3M (2003)
>$500B US telecom bonds issued 1996-2001; >$1T total capital raised since 1998; ~$1.6T all-in financing
Credit shutoff speed: bond market open Jan 2001 -> fully closed Apr 2001 (~4 months)
Junk default rate 5.68% (2000) -> 8.57% (2001); telecom = 18.5% of 2001 defaults; $110B telecom bankruptcies in 18 months
WorldCom Ch.11 Jul 2002: $107B assets / ~$41B debt / $11B fraud; Global Crossing Ch.11 Jan 2002: $22.4B assets / $12.4B debt, resold at ~1-2c/$
Cisco: $555B peak cap Mar 2000, -88% drawdown, 25 years to nominal price recovery; revenue only -15% peak-to-trough
Corning -99%, JDSU -99.7% ($56.1B FY01 loss), Lucent -99.3%, Nortel -99.6%, Level 3 -98%
No new transatlantic cable needed 2003-2015: ~12-year glut absorption at ~2x/yr demand growth
lessons_for_model: Scarcity-rent duration: ~4 years for equipment/component layer (1996/97-2000), ~3 years for the capacity commodity itself (pricing power already eroding by 1999). Calibrate rent half-life after first competitive supply arrives at ~12-18 months.

Supply-response delay: 18-36 months from financing to lit capacity; but add a technology multiplier term — capacity per unit capex rose ~100x in 5 yrs (DWDM), analogous to perf/$ gains in GPUs; supply growth = physical build x tech multiplier, so effective supply can grow 50-100%+/yr per dollar even after capex flattens.

Demand-misperception gain: model believed-demand = actual-demand x 10, with belief persistence ~4 yrs; corruption of the demand signal by vendor financing and revenue round-tripping (swap/circular deals) delayed correction ~1 yr. Include a demand-signal-integrity variable if AI shows circular revenue (chip vendor invests in customer who buys chips).

Capex momentum/overshoot: capex kept accelerating ~1.5-2 yrs AFTER spot prices for the output began falling 40-60%/yr — price signal ignored while capital was available. Overshoot ratio to reproduce: installed potential capacity ~20-50x contemporaneous demand; route/asset-level duplication ~5-10x (N~6 rivals each building for ~100% share).
Bust lag: peak capex (2000) to revenue/price collapse ~1-1.5 yrs; to capex trough 3 yrs (-65%); to bankruptcy wave 1.5-2.5 yrs.

Credit-discipline loop is the binding cutoff, and it is nonlinear: external-finance-dependent builders lost 100% of funding access within ~4 months (Jan->Apr 2001). Key structural difference to encode for 2026 AI: 1990s builders were >70% externally financed (bonds/loans/vendor credit); hyperscalers are majority internal-cash-flow financed — so weaken or delay the credit-cutoff loop for cash-rich players but keep it at full strength for neoclouds/debt-financed datacenter SPVs, the WorldCom-analogues.

Glut-persistence: once overshoot >10x, price never recovers — set commodity-layer price floor at marginal cost indefinitely; glut absorption time = ln(overshoot)/ln(1+demand growth) ~ 10-12 yrs at 2x/yr growth and 20-50x overshoot. Rents in the overbuilt layer are permanently dead, not cyclical.

Rent allocation by layer: un-overbuildable chokepoint (last mile / today: leading-edge fab + power interconnect) keeps rents through the bust; IP/design layer (Cisco / today: Nvidia CUDA) suffers 85-90% multiple compression but keeps franchise if revenue base is sticky; pure capacity (bandwidth / today: undifferentiated GPU-hours) -> equity -98 to -100%, assets recycle at 1-5 cents on the dollar to next-cycle winners.

Equity calibration targets: picks-and-shovels-with-moat drawdown -86 to -89% with revenue only -15% (multiple compression dominates); component suppliers -99%; leveraged capacity operators -100%; nominal price recovery for the surviving moat name: ~25 yrs.
Demand eventually validated the infrastructure (all dark fiber used by ~2010s) but at 95-99% lower unit prices — model must separate volume validation from revenue validation.

Fraud/accounting distortion emerges endogenously in late boom when real demand undershoots promises (WorldCom $11B, Qwest IRU swaps) and extends the boom ~1 yr past fundamentals — consider a reporting-noise term that grows with the gap between promised and realized demand.

episodes.episode: Solar polysilicon boom-bust: spot $475/kg (Mar 2008) to $15.9/kg (Dec 2012); Chinese capacity response destroys scarcity rents
episodes.period: 2004-2013 (scarcity onset 2004; peak price Mar 2008; first crash H2 2008-2009; echo rally 2010; terminal glut Q4 2011-2013; shakeout/defaults 2012-2015)
episodes.bottleneck: Ultra-pure polysilicon feedstock (Siemens-process plants): capital-intensive ($100-150M per 10k MT line era-2008), 18-24 month greenfield build time, closed-club know-how held by 7 incumbents (Hemlock, Wacker, REC, MEMC, Tokuyama, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo). Solar demand grew >600% 2004-2008 against semiconductor-sized supply; price rose ~1000% (spot $28/kg 2003 avg -> $475/kg Mar 2008, 17x).
episodes.capex_overshoot: Capacity multiplied ~10x across the cycle (Bernreuter: 'between the shortage and oversupply periods, production capacity was multiplied by a factor of nearly 10' — from ~30-40k MT global output mid-2000s to ~380-400k MT nameplate by end-2012). 2011 production 255k MT vs demand 230k MT (first surplus year, +25k MT); 2012: production cut to 235k MT, utilization ~60% of nameplate -> capacity/demand ratio ~1.6-1.7x at trough. China's 2007-08 announcement wave alone: 33+ greenfield projects (~140-170k MT announced) vs total world demand then ~50k MT; only ~7-8 Chinese producers still operating by 2013 out of 40-60 entrants. GCL-Poly went 0 -> 65,000 MT (world #1) in 6 years (2006-2012). Incumbents also overshot: Hemlock 36k MT (2010) -> planned 50k (2012) plus $1.2B Clarksville TN plant, completed then never started, written off Dec 2014.

equity_outcomes.name: LDK Solar (wafer->poly integrator, pure capacity play)
equity_outcomes.outcome: IPO Jun 2007 at $27, peak ~$73 Sep 2007; poly production cost $41/kg vs $22.63 spot in 2012; ~$3.5B debt; defaulted on $23.8M convertibles Apr 2013, bankruptcy 2014, liquidated 2016

equity_outcomes.name: Suntech Power (cell/module, capacity play)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Peak ~$86-90 Dec 2007 (largest solar market cap ~$16B); missed $541M convertible payment 15 Mar 2013; Chinese banks holding >$2B forced involuntary insolvency of Wuxi Suntech

equity_outcomes.name: MEMC Electronic Materials (incumbent poly, US)
equity_outcomes.outcome: ~$96 peak 2007 -> ~$1.44 in 2012; exited via SunEdison transformation, which itself went bankrupt 2016

equity_outcomes.name: REC (incumbent poly, Norway)
equity_outcomes.outcome: NOK ~280 (2008) to low single digits; repeated dilutive rescues; Norwegian FBR plants shut 2011-12

equity_outcomes.name: Wacker Chemie (incumbent poly, Germany)
equity_outcomes.outcome: SURVIVED: cost + purity leadership, diversified chemicals; EBITDA margins 50%+ 2008-2011 not sustainable but stayed cash-positive; became world #1 poly maker 2012

equity_outcomes.name: GT Solar / GT Advanced Technologies (poly CVD reactor equipment)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Sold 170+ CVD reactors Jul 2007-Jul 2010, $357.5M poly-equipment revenue FY2010, $519.8M order book — the picks-and-shovels winner of the build-out; orders evaporated 2012 when capex stopped; Chapter 11 Oct 2014

equity_outcomes.name: Centrotherm Photovoltaics (German solar equipment)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Insolvency filing Jul 2012; at least the 14th US/European solar company to founder in the glut

equity_outcomes.name: Applied Materials (equipment, diversified)
equity_outcomes.outcome: SURVIVED via diversification: SunFab thin-film turnkey line amassed $1.5B orders 2007-09 then flamed out; exited SunFab Jul 2010 with ~$400M restructuring; semiconductor core business unharmed. Solar equipment was NOT a durable rent even for the leader

equity_outcomes.name: GCL-Poly (Chinese low-cost entrant)
equity_outcomes.outcome: SURVIVED as new cost leader (~$20/kg cash cost by 2012, 65k MT capacity) but equity still drew down ~85% 2011-2012 and never earned sustained super-rents — took share, not margin

equity_outcomes.name: OCI (Korean entrant)
equity_outcomes.outcome: KRW ~650k (Apr 2011) -> ~60k; survived a decade of breakeven, exited Korean solar poly 2020

episodes.financing_structure: Dual structure. (a) Incumbents (Hemlock, Wacker, OCI): expansions largely pre-funded by CUSTOMER PREPAYMENTS under 6-10 year take-or-pay contracts signed 2006-2008 at fixed high prices, plus internal cash — customers financed the capacity that destroyed their own scarcity premium. (b) Chinese entrants: state-directed bank debt — CDB alone extended ~$43B credit lines to 12 Chinese solar firms in 2010 (~$30.5B+ actually most-active-lender tally; LDK $8.9B, Suntech $7.3B lines); LDK carried ~$3.5B debt at ~250%+ net gearing. Credit tightening did NOT end the boom ex ante: the 2008-09 GFC crunch caused the first spot crash (spot buyers/project finance vanished, -65% in 9 months) but Chinese policy credit kept flowing through 2010-2012, EXTENDING capex ~2 years past the demand signal and deepening the glut. Credit discipline arrived only ex post: banks pulled the plug at Suntech (Mar 2013) and LDK (2013-14) after prices were already below cash cost for ~18 months. Demand-side subsidy cuts (Spain 2.7GW 2008 -> ~0.5GW 2009 cap; German FiT cuts 2010-12) were the proximate demand shock, not lender discipline.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Demand was REALIZED beyond even bull forecasts in volume terms — global PV installs ~1GW (2004) -> ~6GW (2008) -> ~30GW (2012), 30x in 8 years; polysilicon demand grew from ~30k MT to ~230k MT — yet virtually every capacity owner lost money because supply grew ~10x against ~7x demand and the marginal entrant's cost curve reset the price. Canonical case of 'the technology succeeds, the capacity investor still loses.' Prices never recovered: $13-20/kg range persisted 2012-2020 (next scarcity episode only in 2021-22 at ~$40/kg).
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Spot price 17x cost-of-production era: $475/kg spot Mar-Apr 2008 vs incumbent cash cost ~$25-35/kg -> gross margins ~90% on spot sales; industry profit margins cited at 90% at peak; Wacker/OCI EBITDA margins 50-60% even on blended contract prices through 2010-11. Contract prices ($60-100/kg, 6-10yr terms) lagged spot both up and down; spot undercut average contract price from May 2011, breaking the long-term-contract regime (renegotiations, walkaways, Hemlock's contract rigidity cost it market leadership in 2012).
episodes.glut_depth: Price -97% peak-to-trough ($475 Mar 2008 -> $15.35-15.90 Dec 2012); -88% in first 15 months ($475 -> $55 by Jul 2009); 2011 alone -62% ($79 Mar -> <$30 Q4). Trough price below cash cost of ~70% of nameplate capacity (Tier-2 $12/kg realized vs LDK $41/kg cost). Utilization ~60% in 2012 with top-tier producers throttling in Q3 2012. Shakeout: from 40-60 Chinese entrants to ~7-8 producers by 2013; 14+ US/EU solar bankruptcies by mid-2012. Glut duration: prices below reinvestment level ~8 years (2012-2020).
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS (partially, via moat): Wacker (process know-how, purity, semiconductor-grade mix, diversified balance sheet) — compressed but positive margins, became #1; Hemlock survived via parent (Dow Corning) but lost leadership by clinging to contract prices; semiconductor-grade poly (higher purity barrier) stayed rentable throughout. Applied Materials survived because solar was optionality, not the core — but earned NO durable solar rent; its SunFab 'toll' thesis failed in 3 years. Equipment makers' rents (GT Solar 40%+ gross margins on CVD reactors) lasted only as long as the capex flow — one cycle — then went to zero because reactors, once sold, ARE the excess capacity; selling shovels transferred the technology to China and destroyed the sellers' own future market. COMPETED AWAY: every pure-capacity play — LDK, Suntech, REC's solar poly, Tier-2 Chinese poly, thin-film (capacity commoditized before scale). GCL shows the entrant's best case: win on cost, capture share and survival, still no durable super-rent. Durable rent required either purity/process IP + low-cost position (Wacker) or being upstream of the cycle entirely. Nobody kept a toll: polysilicon is fungible, no network effect, no standard lock-in.
key_numbers: Price rise 17x over 4.3 years (2003->Mar 2008); collapse -65% in 9 months, -88% in 15 months, -97% in 4.75 years
Capacity build time: 18-24 months per greenfield Siemens plant (the core supply-response delay)
Capacity multiplied ~10x shortage-to-glut; 2011 first surplus year: 255k MT produced vs 230k MT demand; 2012 utilization ~60%
Long-term contracts: 6-10 year duration with prepayments; spot crossed below contract May 2011 = rent regime break, 3.1 years after spot peak
China entry: 33+ projects announced 2007-08; GCL 0->65k MT in 6 years; survivors 7-8 of 40-60 entrants by 2013
Credit: CDB $43B lines to 12 firms in 2010 (LDK $8.9B, Suntech $7.3B); Suntech default 15 Mar 2013 on $541M converts; LDK default Apr 2013, bankrupt 2014
Peak margins: ~90% gross on spot 2008; Wacker EBITDA 50%+ 2008-2011; trough: LDK cost $41/kg vs $22.63 spot (negative 45% gross)
Demand grew 30x in installs (1GW 2004 -> 30GW 2012) and ~7x in tons, yet returns on capacity went negative — supply response overwhelmed realized hyper-growth
Equipment boom: GT Solar 170+ CVD reactors in 3 years, $519.8M order book Jul 2010 -> orders ~0 by 2012, Ch.11 2014; AMAT SunFab $1.5B orders -> exit in 3 years
Post-bust rent desert: prices $13-20/kg for 8 years (2012-2020) before next shortage (2021-22, ~$40/kg peak)
lessons_for_model: Rent duration structure: SPOT scarcity rents ~4.3 years rising (2004 -> Mar 2008 peak); contract-protected rents extend ~3 more years past spot peak (to May 2011 spot/contract crossover). Model two rent tranches: spot tranche killed by first capacity wave + demand shock at t+4.5; contracted tranche decays over following 3 years then breaks discontinuously (renegotiation/walkaway).

Supply response delay to calibrate: 18-24 months build + ~12 months decision/permitting = ~2.5-3 year total lag from price signal (>3x cost) to first new capacity; full capacity wave lands 4-7 years after signal, i.e., AFTER the price has already crashed — capacity kept arriving 2009-2012 into a falling market (capex momentum loop gain ~1: projects 90%+ completed once started, almost none canceled mid-build except Hemlock Clarksville).

Overshoot magnitude: terminal capacity/demand ~1.6-1.7x; capacity growth ~10x vs demand growth ~7x over the cycle. Announced capacity at peak enthusiasm (2008) was ~3-4x contemporaneous demand — use announcement/demand ratio ~3x as the overshoot driver, with ~60-70% of announcements actually built.

Bust lag: ~1.5 years from peak capex spend (2010-11) to industry-wide sub-cash-cost prices (2012); ~3.5 years from peak PRICE (Mar 2008) to permanent margin destruction (Q4 2011). Echo rally: post-crash demand rebound (2010, price 55->80) re-triggered a second capex wave that deepened the terminal bust — include a second-round overshoot loop.

Credit discipline loop was ABSENT on the way up and arrived ~18-24 months AFTER prices fell below cash cost: state-directed credit ($43B in one year) kept zombie capacity running 2011-2013, lengthening the glut. Calibrate credit-discipline delay at 2 years post-negative-margin, and let policy credit set that delay, not market spreads. The GFC (exogenous credit shock) triggered the FIRST crash but did not stop capex.

Prepayment/take-or-pay financing is a demand-signal amplifier: customers' prepayments funded 30-50% of incumbent expansion capex, converting scarcity fear directly into supply — model prepayments as increasing supply-response gain during scarcity.

Rent-keeper taxonomy for AI/robotics mapping: fungible-output capacity (poly = compute/robot assembly?) retains ZERO rent post-glut and prices at marginal entrant cash cost for ~8 years; process-IP + cost leaders (Wacker/GCL) retain survival + share but only normal returns; equipment/picks-and-shovels rents last exactly ONE capex cycle (~3-4 years of orders) and collapse with capex, with the added dynamic that equipment sales transfer capability to entrants (self-cannibalizing toll); diversified giants (AMAT) treat the boom as an option and exit at ~$0.4-1.5B cost.

Demand realization does not protect returns: model must reproduce simultaneous 30x volume growth and -97% price / negative sector ROIC — i.e., price is set by capacity/demand ratio and marginal cost curve, not by demand growth rate.

Equity calibration: pure-capacity leaders -98% to -100% with 5-7 year peak-to-bankruptcy arc (peak equity Dec 2007, defaults Mar 2013-2014); survivors -75% to -90% drawdowns even with intact franchises; equipment leaders -100% within 4 years of peak order book.

Cost-curve reset: entrant cash costs fell ~50% below incumbent legacy costs within 4 years (GCL ~$20/kg 2012 vs LDK $41, REC Norway shut) — model marginal cost as declining function of cumulative capacity built (learning), which permanently lowers the post-bust price floor and prevents rent recovery for ~8 years.

episodes.episode: US shale oil & gas boom-bust (tight oil revolution): rig/capex boom 2010-2014, first bust 2014-16, zombie re-expansion 2016-18, capital-discipline regime change 2019, terminal bust 2020
episodes.bottleneck: Physical: flowing oil barrels amid perceived global scarcity ($100+ Brent 2011-14, post-peak-oil narrative). Upstream sub-bottlenecks that earned temporary rents: horizontal rigs and pressure-pumping (frac) fleet capacity 2011-14, frac sand 2013-14 and again 2017-18, Permian pipeline takeaway 2018 (Midland-Cushing differential blew out to -$15/bbl). Permanent bottleneck: irreplaceable Tier-1 acreage/mineral rights (core Permian/Delaware geology) — the only input that could not be manufactured.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Rigs: peak 1,931 total US rigs (1,609 oil rigs, Oct 2014) vs ~500-650 rigs sufficient by 2017 to hold/grow output after productivity gains — ~3x physical-capacity overshoot. Capex: global E&P capex peaked at $780B in 2014, then cut $200B (2015) + $140B (2016) = -44%; US onshore fell ~$150B (2014) to ~$60B (2016), -60%. Supply vs demand: US crude grew ~+1.0 mb/d/yr 2012-2014 (5.0 mb/d 2008 → 9.6 mb/d Apr-2015 → 13.0 mb/d Nov-2019) while global demand grew only ~1.2-1.5 mb/d/yr total; resulting global oversupply of ~1.7-2.0 mb/d = only ~2% of 94 mb/d demand was enough to crash price 76%. Hidden inventory overhang: ~8,800 drilled-uncompleted (DUC) wells at 2019 peak ≈ 1 extra year of supply already paid for.

episodes.financing_structure: Overwhelmingly external. Cumulative negative free cash flow: a 30-producer cross-section outspent cash flow by $158B (2010-2019); industry-wide estimates $250-300B+; FCF negative EVERY year 2010-2019. Funded by: (1) high-yield bonds — energy went from 8% to 16% of the US HY market by 2014; ~$290B of HY energy issuance 2008-2014 (15% of all HY issuance); E&P net debt $15.6B (1998) to $244B (mid-2014); (2) reserve-based lending (RBL) bank revolvers, cut brutally in semiannual borrowing-base redeterminations 2015-16; (3) repeated equity issuance ($60B+ of follow-ons 2015-16 alone bailed out the first bust). Credit-crunch role: HY energy OAS went ~350bp (mid-2014) to 1,600-2,000bp (Feb 2016) — refinancing shut, driving the 2015-16 bankruptcy wave. BUT cheap capital reopened in 2016-17 and refunded a second drilling ramp at $50 oil — the boom did NOT die of the 2014 price signal. It died when capital markets closed permanently: zero shale public offerings after late-2018, investors demanding FCF/dividends over growth in 2019, then COVID. Terminal toll (Haynes & Boone, 2015-2021): 274 E&P + 330 oilfield-service/midstream bankruptcies, >$321B of debt.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Demand fully delivered — this was a pure supply-overshoot bust. Global oil demand grew from ~89 mb/d (2010) to ~100 mb/d (2019), right on forecast (~1.2-1.5 mb/d/yr). The 'peak oil scarcity' narrative failed on the supply side, not demand: US supply alone grew +8 mb/d 2008-2019, absorbing most of a decade of global demand growth. A mere ~2% global oversupply (1.7-2.0 mb/d, 2015-16) collapsed price 76%. The 2020 leg was a demand shock (-20 mb/d for weeks, WTI printed -$37.63 on 4/20/2020) hitting an already-glutted, credit-starved system.
episodes.glut_depth: 2015-16: ~1.7-2.0 mb/d oversupply (~2% of demand); OECD inventories ~380-420 Mbbl above 5-yr average; WTI $107 (Jun 2014) to $26.19 (Feb 11, 2016) = -76%; rigs -79% (1,931 to 404 May 2016). Frac fleet utilization ~50-60% in 2016, ~40% in 2020. 2020: WTI -$37.63 intraday; oil rigs bottomed at 172 (Aug 2020), -89% vs 2014. Well costs fell ~40% 2014-16 — deflation passed through to customers, not retained as margin.
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Brent averaged ~$111/bbl 2011-2013 (>$100 sustained ~3.5 yrs, Feb 2011-Sep 2014) vs shale full-cycle breakevens of $60-80 then — implied wellhead 'scarcity margin' of 30-60%. Land rig dayrates ~$27-28k (2014) vs ~$17k (2016). Pressure-pumping EBITDA margins ~20%+ (2014) to negative (2016). Frac sand spot ~$70-80/ton (2014, again 2017) to ~$15-25/ton after in-basin capacity entry. Permian royalty acreage values rose ~10x 2010-2019 — the rent migrated to the unreproducible input.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT RENTS (toll/royalty/scarce-input owners): mineral & royalty owners (TPL, Viper, Black Stone) — perpetual 12.5-25% revenue share, zero capex, zero opex exposure; Tier-1 acreage E&Ps (EOG, Pioneer, Diamondback) — geology as moat; take-or-pay midstream contracts (partially — Alerian MLP index still -60%+ where contracts were volume-exposed). COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity, no IP protection): pressure pumpers, frac sand, offshore/land drillers, marginal-acreage E&Ps — all saw returns driven to/below zero within ~2 years of each capacity ramp. Critically, shale had NO durable technology moat: fracking/drilling innovations (pad drilling, longer laterals, higher sand loading) diffused across the industry in 1-3 years via service companies and personnel mobility, so 'tech leader' rents decayed fast; the productivity gains (rig productivity roughly tripling 2014-16, e.g. ND wells/rig/month 0.8 in 2012 to 1.4 in 2016) accrued to consumers as lower prices and to royalty owners, not to innovators. Even the 'AI-like tech premium' names (SLB digital) ended -90%.

lessons_for_model: Supply-response delay killing scarcity rents: ~4 years from sustained price signal (late-2010 $90+ oil) to price collapse (Nov 2014). Calibrate scarcity-rent duration for manufacturable capacity at 3.5-4.5 yrs; if the AI analog (fab/DC buildout) has 2-3 yr construction lags, expect similar 4±1 yr rent window from capex ignition.

Capex-momentum/overshoot loop: output peaked 6 months AFTER the price bust and physical capacity overshot need by ~3x (rigs). Model should reproduce: capacity additions continue 0.5-1.0 yr past the price break; peak capacity ~2.5-3x demand-consistent capacity in the bottlenecked input (rigs/fleets), even when final-output overshoot is small (~2%).

Tiny glut, huge price move: -76% price on ~2% oversupply. Use a highly convex price function near capacity balance: local elasticity such that 1% excess supply -> 20-40% price decline for commodity-like outputs (undifferentiated compute/tokens would behave the same).

Efficiency paradox (Jevons on the supply side): during the bust, productivity per unit capex rose 30-75%, so output fell only 12% while capex fell 60% — capacity effectively KEEPS GROWING through the bust. Model must include a learning-curve term that accelerates during downturns (high-grading), which deepens and lengthens the glut.

Credit-discipline loop is the true off-switch, with long delay: first credit shock (2015-16, spreads 350->1,800bp) did NOT end the boom — markets reopened within 12-18 months and refunded a second ramp. The boom ended only after ~5 years of negative FCF when equity+debt windows closed simultaneously (2019). Calibrate: external-financing share of capex ~30-50% at peak; credit shutoff threshold when spreads >1,000bp AND cumulative sector FCF deficit >~1.5x annual sector revenue; two credit cycles before terminal discipline.

Rent allocation for calibration: (a) unreproducible input owners (land/royalty ~ IP, foundational-model moats, prime power/interconnection rights in the AI analog) keep rents indefinitely and compound through the bust (TPL +900% while operators -90%); (b) tech-leader rents decay with diffusion half-life ~1.5-3 yrs absent IP protection; (c) pure-capacity rents (fleets ~ commodity GPUs-for-rent, neoclouds) last <2 yrs per cycle and go to zero at trough utilization 40-60%.
Bust lag: peak-capex-to-price-bust ~0.4 yr; peak-capex-to-bankruptcy-wave ~1.5 yr; peak-capex-to-capitulation/consolidation ~5-6 yrs (2014->2020). Use three-stage bust in the model.

Deflation pass-through: 40% unit-cost declines were fully competed through to output price within ~2 yrs; do not let cost curves improve margins for undifferentiated producers in the model — route the surplus to consumers and to bottleneck-input owners.

Demand delivering on forecast does NOT protect returns: demand grew exactly as promised (+11 mb/d over the decade) yet sector equity fell 90%. In the model, decouple demand realization from producer returns; producer returns should load on the supply-side overshoot ratio and financing structure, not on demand growth.

episodes.period: 2016-2024 (three nested cycles: crypto-GPU 2017-19, crypto-GPU/ASIC 2020-22, AI compute 2023-24+)
episodes.bottleneck: Sequentially migrating physical constraint: (1) 2017-18 & 2020-22: GPU/ASIC unit supply (foundry allocation + rig assembly, 6-12 mo order-to-delivery); (2) Mar 2023: leading-edge GPU dies (H100 lead time 52 weeks late 2023); (3) mid-2023-2024: TSMC CoWoS advanced packaging (13k wafers/mo end-2023, the binding constraint on H100 output); (4) 2024-25: HBM memory (SK Hynix/Micron sold out 2024 AND 2025 by mid-2024); (5) emerging 2025: datacenter power/shells. Rents accrued to whoever owned the currently-binding stage.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Commodity-capacity layer overshot 1.5-2.0x demand-consistent capacity in both crypto busts. (a) 2022 Bitcoin: network hashrate kept growing ~+40% through 2022 (to ~250 EH/s Dec 2022) while BTC fell 65-75%, because rigs ordered 9-12 months earlier at the Nov 2021 peak kept arriving — hash price fell 85% ($0.40 to ~$0.06/TH/day), implying ~1.6-1.7x capacity vs breakeven-consistent at $17k BTC. (b) Ethereum GPU fleet: hashrate ~1.05 PH/s May 2022 (~$10-15B of GPUs, est. 15-25M cards) stranded to zero value at the Sept 15, 2022 Merge — 100% overshoot at that layer. (c) NVDA channel: gaming sell-in ran ~1.6x true sell-through by mid-2022; $1.32B inventory charge Q2 FY23 + further charges = ~$2.2B FY23, roughly one quarter of segment revenue. (d) 2018 analog: crypto OEM revenue $289M Q1 FY19 collapsed to ~$18M by Q2 FY19 (vs ~$100M guided); Q4 FY19 guidance cut $2.7B to $2.2B (-19%), $57M writedown, gaming rev -45% YoY. (e) Memory 2022-23: DRAM inventory ~30+ weeks vs 8-10 normal (~3x), industry capex cut 40-50% in 2023 — then HBM shortage flipped memory back to record margins within 18 months.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: Crypto cycles: promised structural demand ('mining is permanent') realized at approximately -100% — Ethereum PoS merge (Sep 2022) deleted the entire GPU-mining demand source overnight; BTC mining demand fell ~85% in revenue-per-capacity terms. AI cycle: demand realized ABOVE promise through 2024 — NVDA data center revenue $15.0B FY2023 -> $47.5B FY2024 -> $115.2B FY2025 (7.7x in 2 years); total FY2025 revenue $130.5B (+114% YoY); this over-realization is why no bust occurred by end-2024 despite 2x/yr supply growth — the bottleneck migrated (CoWoS -> HBM -> power) instead of clearing. Hyperscaler capex (MSFT+GOOGL+AMZN+META) ~$147B 2023 -> ~$220B+ 2024, absorbed by realized inference/training demand.
episodes.glut_depth: Price undershoot at commodity layer after each bust: used RTX 3080s fell from ~2.0-2.6x MSRP street price (peak premium +157% on RTX 3060 Ti class, cards listed at $1,199-$3,000 vs $699 MSRP) to BELOW MSRP ($523 listings) within ~4 months of the Merge — a ~70-75% fall from peak street price. Bitmain S19-class rig prices -80-85% ($10-12k Nov 2021 -> $1.5-2k late 2022). Hash price -85%. DRAM spot -50%+ in 2022-23 (worst memory downturn since 2008; SK Hynix quarterly operating losses ~W3.4T in H1 2023). NVDA GAAP gross margin trough 43.5% (Q2 FY2023) vs ~65% normal — a 21-pt margin undershoot lasting 2 quarters.
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: NVDA GAAP gross margin path: ~59-60% 2017-18 crypto peak -> 54.7% Q4 FY19 bust -> ~65% 2021 -> 43.5% Q2 FY23 trough -> 64.6% Q1 FY24 -> 78.4% Q1 FY25 peak (Apr 2024) -> ~73-75% as Blackwell ramped; FY2025 full-year 75.0%. H100 ASP $25-40k vs est. BOM ~$3-4k (~85-90% product-level margin). H100 cloud rental $8/hr mid-2023 -> ~$2/hr late 2024 (rental-layer rents competed away in ~18 months even while NVDA hardware margins held). TSMC: GM 51.6% 2021 -> 59.6% 2022 (record, +8pp on price hikes) -> ~54.4% 2023 dip -> recovering 2024; wafer prices N5 ~$16k -> N4/N5 +~25% cumulative since 2021, N3 $18-20k; announced hikes: up to 20% (Aug 2021), ~6% (2022), ~10% advanced nodes (2024-25). HBM: 5-6x price premium per GB vs DDR5; HBM3E ~$300/stack; sold out 2024+2025 by mid-2024; +20% price hikes accepted for 2026.
episodes.financing_structure: Bifurcated, and this is the key structural finding. CORE (NVDA, TSMC, hyperscalers, Samsung/Hynix): almost entirely internal cash flow — NVDA prepaid ~$9B multi-year supply commitments from its own balance sheet; hyperscaler 2023-24 AI capex (~$147B->$220B+) funded from ~$300-400B combined operating cash flow, zero net leverage. FRINGE (pure-capacity operators): heavily levered — public bitcoin miners raised ~$6B equity + ~$4B debt in 2021 alone, much of it rig-collateralized equipment financing at 10-15% rates; Core Scientific carried ~$1.3B+ debt (liabilities filed $1-10B), Marathon $747M converts; AI-era analog: CoreWeave's GPU-collateralized debt ($2.3B Aug 2023 at ~10-14%, $7.5B May 2024). DID CREDIT TIGHTENING END THE BOOM? No — demand-price collapse was the trigger in both crypto busts (BTC -75%, Merge); 2022 Fed tightening + energy cost spikes were AMPLIFIERS that converted a margin squeeze into ~20+ bankruptcies (Compute North Sep 2022, $500M owed; Core Scientific Ch.11 Dec 2022 with ~10% of network hashrate, 143k rigs; Celsius Mining; Argo near-bankruptcy) because rig collateral fell 80-85%, freezing refinancing. Internally-financed players never faced a financing constraint — they took inventory writedowns and kept investing.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT DURABLE RENTS (IP/moat/toll): NVDA — CUDA software lock-in; GM returned above prior peak after BOTH busts (43.5% trough -> 78.4% peak in 7 quarters); stock -56% (Oct-Dec 2018) and -66% (Nov 2021-Oct 2022) but recovered to new highs within ~2 years each time, then 10x. TSMC — process-node monopoly toll; GM never below ~53% even in 2023 downturn, raised prices INTO the downturn. SK Hynix — HBM qualification moat (12-18 mo customer qual cycle = de facto 2-yr exclusivity on HBM3 for NVDA); from record losses H1 2023 to record profits 2024. COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity, no moat): bitcoin miners — Core Scientific (SPAC ~$4.3B EV Jul 2021, -98% 2022, Ch.11 Dec 2022, emerged Jan 2024 wiping equity), Compute North (bankrupt Sep 2022), Marathon/Riot -90 to -95% drawdowns; rig makers — Bitmain (cancelled 2018 IPO, ~50% layoffs Dec 2018), Canaan (IPO Nov 2019 at $9, -80% within months); GPU cloud rental layer — H100 rental rates -75% in 18 months; AIB partners (EVGA exited GPU business Sep 2022 citing zero margins). Rule confirmed: rents survive where there is a software ecosystem, process monopoly, or qualification barrier; rents die in <2 years where capacity is fungible.

Moat/toll rents last 3+ years to indefinite (NVDA GM >70% for 3+ yrs; TSMC GM floor 53%; HBM oligopoly 3+ yrs, protected by 12-18 mo qualification cycle). Model needs two rent-decay time constants: tau_commodity ~1.5y, tau_moat >5y.

SUPPLY-RESPONSE DELAY: 12-18 months from price signal to capacity online (rig order-to-delivery 9-12 mo; H100 lead time normalized 52->10 wks in ~12 mo; CoWoS capacity doubles with ~12 mo lag; HBM qualification 12-18 mo). Use pipeline delay of 1.0-1.5y in the supply loop.

CAPEX MOMENTUM/OVERSHOOT LOOP GAIN: capacity continues growing 9-12 months AFTER the price signal reverses (BTC hashrate +40% in 2022 during -65% price fall). Peak capacity lands at 1.5-2.0x demand-consistent level at the commodity layer. Calibrate momentum such that in-flight orders equal ~1 year of peak-rate installs.

BUST LAG: 0.75-1.25 years from capex-commitment peak to writedowns/bankruptcies (Nov 2021 peak -> Sep-Dec 2022 bankruptcies = 10-13 mo; Q1-2018 GPU channel peak -> Nov 2018 bust = ~9 mo). Target ~1.0y.

PRICE UNDERSHOOT IN GLUT: -70 to -85% from peak at commodity layer (hash price -85%, rigs -80-85%, GPU street -70-75%, DRAM -50%); producer margin swings ~20+ pts (NVDA GM 65->43.5%) but only for 2-3 quarters; writedown magnitude ~1 quarter of segment revenue.

CREDIT-DISCIPLINE LOOP: applies ONLY to the leveraged fringe (~15-25% of cycle capex - miners, neoclouds), which finances at 10-15% against equipment collateral that falls 80%+ in the bust; the core (NVDA, TSMC, hyperscalers) is internally financed and never faces a financing constraint. Credit tightening AMPLIFIED but did not TRIGGER either bust - demand collapse did. For 2026-36 model: credit crunch is a fringe-clearing mechanism and second-order for aggregate capex unless leverage share rises.

BOTTLENECK MIGRATION: when demand over-realizes, rents migrate to the next constraint every 12-18 months (GPU dies 2023 -> CoWoS mid-2023-24 -> HBM 2024-25 -> power 2025+) rather than dissipating in aggregate. A one-bottleneck model will wrongly predict rent collapse when the first constraint clears; model a chain of 3-4 sequential constraints with staggered supply-response delays.

DEMAND-REALIZATION IS THE BUST SWITCH: crypto demand realized at ~-100% of promise (Merge = exogenous demand deletion) -> immediate bust; AI demand realized ABOVE promise 2023-24 (NVDA DC rev 7.7x in 2 yrs) -> no bust despite supply doubling annually. Model bust probability should key off (realized demand growth) minus (capacity growth ~2x/yr), not off capacity growth alone.

EQUITY OUTCOME DISTRIBUTION: moat firms draw down -50 to -66% and recover to new highs in ~2y; pure-capacity firms draw down -90 to -98% with ~30% bankruptcy/restructure rate and permanent equity impairment; intermediary/assembly layer (AIBs, EVGA) captures ~zero rent even at peak scarcity.

TOLL-COLLECTOR PRICING POWER IS COUNTERCYCLICAL-RESISTANT: TSMC raised prices up to 20% into the 2021 shortage AND held/raised prices through the 2023 utilization dip; monopoly toll GM band 53-60% across the whole cycle. Model the foundry/toll node with near-zero rent decay and price ratchet (hikes stick).

episodes.episode: Japan bubble economy: Plaza Accord to banking-crisis workout — credit/collateral-driven capex boom where the demand thesis (Japanese manufacturing wins globally) was substantially TRUE but was overpaid for by 3-5x via a land-collateral credit loop
episodes.period: 1985-1995 core (Plaza Accord Sep 22, 1985 → asset peak Dec 1989/land peak 1991 → capex trough 1994); full workout extends to 1997-2003 banking crisis and NPL disposal through 2004
episodes.bottleneck: Two-layer bottleneck. (1) Urban land — absolutely fixed supply, doubling as the collateral base for the entire credit system; commercial land in the 6 largest cities rose ~4x 1985-1991 (~13%/yr nationwide); total Japan land value reached ~¥2,000-2,400 trillion at end-1989 (~5x GDP, ~4x the value of ALL US land on a landmass 1/25th the size). Land was the toll asset: whoever held it could borrow against it, creating the loop. (2) Manufacturing capacity/labor scarcity 1988-1991: Tankan capacity-DI showed shortage (~-25), job-offers-to-applicants ratio hit 1.4; DRAM-specific scarcity 1987-88 after the 1986 US-Japan Semiconductor Agreement price floors — DRAM prices roughly tripled 1987-88 and Japanese makers (51% of world semis in 1988, ~90% of 1Mb DRAM) earned windfall rents that financed the next fab generation.
episodes.capex_overshoot: Private non-residential fixed investment rose from ~14% of GDP (1986) to ~19-20% of GDP at peak (FY1990-91) — an overshoot ratio of ~1.35-1.4x versus the demand-consistent pre/post-boom norm of ~14-15%. Total gross fixed capital formation peaked ~32.5% of GDP in 1990-91. Real business investment grew ~+15%/yr in 1988-89 while real GDP grew 5% — investment contributed 2.75pp of the 5% GDP growth 1987-90. Post-bust, plant & equipment spending fell ~4.5% of GDP (IMF), i.e. ~75% retracement of the boom-era rise. Capital coefficient (K/Y) rose from ~1.6 to ~2.0; excess capital stock in the mid-1990s estimated at ¥60-90 trillion (12-18% of GDP). Tankan capacity DI swung ~50 points, from roughly -25 (shortage, 1989-90) to +28 (excess, 1993-94). The excess capacity ("three excesses": capacity, debt, employment) was not fully worked off until 2002-2005.

equity_outcomes.name: Nikkei 225
equity_outcomes.outcome: Peak 38,915.87 on Dec 29, 1989 (TSE cap $4.1T = 1.5x GDP, ~45% of world equity cap). -48% within 12 months of tightening; -63% by Aug 1992 (14,309); ultimate trough 7,055 in Mar 2009 (-82%). Did not regain Dec-1989 peak until Feb 22, 2024 — 34.2 years.

equity_outcomes.name: TOPIX Banks / credit-loop institutions
equity_outcomes.outcome: Pure collateral-loop plays annihilated: bank index ~-93% peak (1989) to trough (2003). LTCB nationalized Oct 1998 (equity ~100% wiped), Nippon Credit Bank nationalized Dec 1998, Hokkaido Takushoku failed Nov 1997, Yamaichi Securities (4th-largest broker) collapsed Nov 1997. Jusen housing lenders (¥13T loan book) liquidated 1996 with ¥6.4T losses.

equity_outcomes.name: NTT
equity_outcomes.outcome: Poster child of overpaying for a real franchise: IPO Feb 1987 at ¥1.19M, peak ¥3.18M Apr 1987 (P/E ~250, briefly worth more than West Germany's entire market). Fell ~73%; never regained its 1987 peak. Business remained a profitable toll — the entry price destroyed 3+ decades of returns.

equity_outcomes.name: NEC / DRAM makers (Toshiba, Hitachi, Fujitsu, Mitsubishi memory ops)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Won the technology race, lost the capacity race. World #1 semis 1985-1991; Japan share 51% (1988) → ~29% (1998) → ~10% (2010s). Samsung/Hyundai replicated capacity with cheaper capital; Korea passed Japan in DRAM 1998. NEC+Hitachi DRAM merged into Elpida 1999; Elpida bankrupt Feb 2012 (¥448B / $5.5B, largest Japanese manufacturer bankruptcy). NEC stock ~-90% peak to 2012.

equity_outcomes.name: Mitsubishi Estate / property developers
equity_outcomes.outcome: Bought Rockefeller Center Oct 1989 for $1.4B at the exact top; walked away 1995 writing off ~$2B. Urban commercial land -87% from 1991 peak to 2005 trough; developer equities -80%+ and dead money for a decade despite owning 'scarce' Marunouchi land — the toll survived, the leveraged entry price didn't.

equity_outcomes.name: Toyota / Honda
equity_outcomes.outcome: Demand thesis winners: ~-50-55% drawdown 1990-93 but recovered to new highs by late 1990s. Kept and grew global auto share through the entire lost decade (manufacturing IP, brand, Toyota Production System = process moat). Balance sheets were cash-rich, not collateral-levered.

equity_outcomes.name: Fanuc / Keyence / Murata / Shin-Etsu / Tokyo Electron (IP-toll upstream)
equity_outcomes.outcome: Component, materials, and equipment toll positions with 30-50% operating margins: drew down with the index but compounded to many multiples of 1989 prices over the following decades. The durable rents in the episode sat upstream (equipment/materials/components), not in end-capacity.

key_numbers: Plaza Accord Sep 22, 1985: yen 240/USD → 120 by end-1987; BOJ cut discount rate 5.0% → 2.5% (Feb 1987), held 27 months — the fuel
BOJ official discount rate raised 2.5% → 6.0% in five steps, May 1989-Aug 1990 (+350bp in 15 months); MOF 'soryo-kisei' quantitative cap on real-estate lending April 1990 — the pin
Nikkei peak Dec 29, 1989 = 38,915.87; 3.1x its Sep-1985 level; TSE market cap $4.1T (1.5x GDP) vs $0.9T (0.6x GDP) end-1985
Land: +13%/yr nationwide 1985-90; 6-city commercial index ~4x 1985-91; total land value ~¥2,000-2,400T ≈ 5x GDP ≈ 4x all US land; urban land then fell >80% 1991-2002 (6-city commercial -87% to 2005)

Private nonresidential investment: ~14% GDP (1986) → ~19-20% GDP (FY1990-91 peak) → fell ~4.5pp of GDP by 1994; real business investment +15%/yr 1988-89, then -1%/-10%/-5% in 1992/93/94 (~-18% cumulative)
Official business cycle: expansion 1986Q4-1991Q1 (51 months); capex peaked ~5 quarters AFTER the Nikkei peak and ~3 quarters after credit was capped — capex momentum

Corporate external financing 1985-90: ~¥85T raised; 1989 alone ~¥26T of equity + equity-linked (warrant/convertible) issuance at 0-2% coupons, swapped to sub-LIBOR — perceived near-zero/negative cost of capital; zaitech profits exceeded operating profits at some majors

Bank credit grew ~9-10%/yr 1986-90 vs nominal GDP ~6.5%/yr; private credit/GDP rose ~25pp; real-estate + construction + nonbank ('three bubble sectors') reached ~25% of bank loans; jusen loan book ¥13T
Semiconductors: Japan 51% world share 1988 (NEC #1, 90% of 1Mb DRAM); Korea passed Japan in DRAM 1998 — ~10 years from peak share to dethronement, ~5-7 years for entrant capacity to bite

Aftermath: cumulative NPL disposals ¥96.4T FY1992-2004 (~19% of GDP); total paper wealth destroyed est. >¥1,000-1,500T (2-3x GDP); GDP growth 5% (1987-90) → ~1%/yr (1992-2002); banking crisis peaked 1997-98, 8 years after asset peak

Manufacturing current-profit margins peaked FY1989 (~4.5% of sales, ~2x 1986), normalized to ~2.5% by FY1992-93 — scarcity rents lasted ~4-5 years (FY1987-FY1991); DRAM-specific windfall rents only ~2-3 years (1987-89) before Korean supply response
episodes.peak_margin_or_price_signal: Manufacturing current profits roughly doubled FY1986-FY1989 (current profit/sales ~4.5% at peak vs ~2.5% norm); Tankan capacity DI at ~-25 (shortage) and job-offers ratio 1.4 signaled scarcity 1988-90. DRAM prices ~tripled 1987-88 post-Semiconductor Agreement. Land: 13%/yr appreciation with rental yields in central Tokyo compressed below 1% — price-to-income for Tokyo condos >18x; Nikkei P/E ~60x, NTT P/E ~250x. The price signal was dominated by collateral value, not cash yield — the key pathology.
episodes.financing_structure: Predominantly EXTERNAL and collateral-levered, in two channels. (1) Bank debt against land collateral: bank lending +9-10%/yr, real-estate-linked sectors to ~25% of loan books; rising land prices expanded collateral capacity which expanded lending which raised land prices — a positive loop with ~13%/yr collateral appreciation feeding ~1.5x credit-to-NGDP growth. (2) Equity-linked capital markets: ¥85T external raise 1985-90; warrant/convertible bonds at 0-2% coupons issued into a rising stock market — firms perceived cost of capital as ~zero and ran zaitech carry trades (borrow via warrants, park in tokkin funds holding stocks), making the financing loop self-referential: issuance propped stocks which cheapened issuance. Internal cash mattered less at the margin; capex hurdle rates collapsed. CREDIT TIGHTENING UNAMBIGUOUSLY ENDED THE BOOM: it did not die of demand exhaustion — BOJ +350bp (May 1989-Aug 1990) plus the April 1990 MOF quantitative cap on real-estate lending; equities fell 48% within 12 months of the first hike, equity-linked refinancing froze (¥ trillions of warrant bonds needed cash redemption 1992-94 instead of conversion), the collateral loop ran in reverse, and capex followed with a ~5-quarter lag.
episodes.demand_realized_vs_promised: The demand thesis was REAL but realized at roughly one-quarter of the priced-in rate. Promised: 'Japan as Number One' — 4-5% perpetual GDP growth, Japanese dominance of autos, electronics, semis, finance; asset prices at 1989 discounted essentially permanent 1987-89 conditions. Realized: Japanese autos DID win globally (Toyota became world #1), electronics/components/materials DID keep large global positions, exports kept growing — but GDP grew ~1%/yr 1992-2002 vs ~4%+ implied, and the specific capacity-intensive businesses (DRAM) lost to cheaper-capital entrants within a decade despite technical leadership. Net: paying 3-5x demand-consistent asset values for a true growth story still produced 60-90% drawdowns and 10-34 year recovery times. Overpaying converted a correct thesis into a lost decade.
episodes.glut_depth: Capacity: Tankan capacity DI swung from ~-25 (shortage) to +28 (excess); excess capital stock ¥60-90T (12-18% of GDP); manufacturing capacity utilization fell ~15-20% 1991-94; excess capacity not cleared until 2002-05 (10+ years). Prices: urban commercial land -80% to -87% over 11-14 years; Nikkei -63% in 2.7 years, -82% to final trough; 16Mb DRAM fell ~80% in 1996 alone during the Korean-supply glut. Credit: ¥96.4T NPLs disposed over 12 years; bank lending growth ~0% by 1993-94 and negative in the late 1990s.
episodes.survivors_vs_casualties: KEPT DURABLE RENTS (IP/moat/toll): (a) process-IP manufacturers — Toyota, Honda (production-system moat, brand; recovered to new highs by mid-late 1990s); (b) upstream toll positions — Fanuc (CNC/robotics, 40%+ margins), Keyence, Murata/TDK (components), Shin-Etsu (wafers), Tokyo Electron (semicap), Nintendo (content IP) — the equipment/materials/components layer kept pricing power even as their capacity-owning customers bled; (c) unlevered cash-rich balance sheets generally. COMPETED AWAY (pure capacity / collateral plays): (a) DRAM fabs — world-best technology, 51% world share, destroyed by Samsung/Hyundai capacity replication in ~5-7 years; commodity output + capex arms race = zero durable rent; (b) banks/brokers/jusen — balance-sheet commodity businesses whose 'moat' was the collateral loop itself (LTCB, NCB, Yamaichi, Hokkaido Takushoku all dead 1997-98); (c) real-estate developers and general contractors — owned the scarce asset but at leveraged 1989 prices; (d) steel/shipbuilding/petchem capacity. PATTERN FOR THE AI MODEL: rents migrated one layer upstream of the capacity being overbuilt (the 'sell shovels' layer) and to holders of non-replicable process IP; anything replicable with capital was replicated within one investment cycle (~5-7 years) by entrants with cheaper capital.
lessons_for_model: Capex-momentum delay: real capex peaked 5 quarters AFTER the financial-asset peak (Nikkei Dec 1989 → capex peak 1991Q1) and 3 quarters after credit was administratively capped (Apr 1990). Calibrate the capex-pipeline inertia at ~1.25 years — orders/projects in flight complete even after financing conditions reverse.

Scarcity-rent duration: economy-wide super-normal margins lasted ~4.5 years (FY1987-FY1991, margin peak FY1989, normalized FY1992); commodity-tech-specific rents (DRAM) only 2-3 years before entrant supply response. Model rent half-life for replicable capacity at 2-3 years once rivals commit capex; 4-5 years for the aggregate.

Supply-response/replication delay for capacity rents: an entrant with cheaper capital (Samsung, entered DRAM at scale ~1985-88) fully dethroned the incumbent in ~10 years and materially compressed margins within ~5-7 years (~2 fab generations). Use 5-7 yr as the competed-away timescale for pure-capacity rents.

Capex overshoot amplitude: peak investment/GDP ran ~1.35-1.4x the demand-consistent level (14% → 19-20% of GDP over 5 yrs), then retraced ~75% of the rise in 3 years. Capital-stock overhang 12-18% of GDP took 10+ years to absorb at ~1% demand growth. Overhang absorption time ≈ overhang / (realized demand growth) — slow demand growth makes gluts decade-long.

Collateral-credit loop gain: land +13%/yr → credit growth 1.5x nominal GDP growth → credit/GDP +25pp in 5 yrs → land +13%/yr. The loop gain >1 while policy rate ≤2.5%; loop reversed within 2-4 quarters of the quantitative lending cap. In the AI analogue: model compute/GPU-backed or market-cap-backed borrowing as the equivalent collateral channel, and make the boom's end a credit-policy event, not a demand event.

Credit discipline arrived exogenously and late: +350bp over 15 months plus a hard quantitative cap killed the boom; equities -48% within 12 months of the first hike. Calibrate: boom persists as long as real cost of capital stays near zero regardless of margin evidence; the bust trigger is financing-side, and the boom had already run ~2 years past the point where yields/margins justified prices.

Overpaying for a TRUE demand thesis: realized demand growth was ~25% of priced-in growth (1%/yr vs ~4%+). Even correct technology/demand bets produced -60% to -90% equity outcomes when entry prices assumed permanence of scarcity rents. Model should separate 'thesis correctness' from 'rent durability' — they were uncorrelated for capacity owners.

Rent allocation for the 2026-36 analogue: durable rents accrued to (i) upstream equipment/materials/component tolls and (ii) process-IP holders with unlevered balance sheets; ~0% durable rents to leveraged owners of the scarce asset itself and to commodity-capacity operators. Weight terminal-rent distribution accordingly (e.g., semicap/materials-analogue keeps margins; GPU-farm/datacenter-capacity-analogue mean-reverts to cost of capital in ~5 yrs).

Bust asymmetry and workout delays: boom 5 yrs; asset-price peak → real-economy trough 4 yrs; → banking-system crisis 8 yrs (evergreening delayed loss recognition); NPL disposal ¥96.4T over 12 yrs ≈ 1.5-2% of GDP/yr drag. If credit losses are socialized/hidden, extend the model's post-bust stagnation to ~2.5x the boom length.

Utilization/DI swing target: capacity-sentiment indicator should swing ~50 points (from -25 shortage to +28 excess) over ~4 years across the peak; capacity utilization -15-20%; downstream commodity output prices (DRAM analogue = GPU-hour/token prices) should be capable of -80% in a single glut year once entrant supply lands.

Recovery-time targets for validation: broad equity index -63% in <3 yrs, 34 yrs to nominal recovery; scarce-asset (land) -80%+ over 11-14 yrs with NO bubble-peak recovery; winner equities (Toyota-analogue) -50% but new highs within 5-7 yrs. A calibrated model should reproduce this three-way dispersion from a single boom.

base_rates: S&P 500 drawdown >20%: 14 episodes / 100 yrs -> 1.4 per decade; ~13% probability a new one starts in any given year; 9 of 10 decades contained at least one (only the 1990s escaped, and only by 0.1pp) -> P(>=1 per decade) ~ 90%
S&P 500 drawdown >40% (bust-class): 5 episodes (1929, 1937, 1973, 2000, 2007) -> 0.5 per decade; ~5%/yr; clustered after valuation (CAPE>30) plus capex/credit booms

Credit crunch / spread blowout (HY OAS >800bp or Baa spread >400bp or systemic bank funding stress): ~10-12 episodes / 100 yrs -> ~1.1 per decade; ~10%/yr unconditional; conditional on Fed tightening cycle underway, roughly 1-in-3; post-2008, median time-to-normalization compressed from ~2-3 yrs to ~2-6 months due to central-bank backstops
